TO A CUCKOO. Most intelligent bird! For you know your own name, .3 And you win all your fame, By repeating one word, Cuckoo, only cuckoo! As you ffy like a hawk, From hedgerow to hedgerow, With a hawk's spirit too Of yourself is your talk, Cuckoo, only cuckoo! With Satanic-like zest— Though the sound from your Cbsfit, Soft as turtle dove's coo— You will steal a bird's nest, Chanting, cuckoo. cuckeel There are cuckoos my way Oft experience brings Without any wings, And face like a man's, • Speaking softly as you. With similar plans, As bad if not worse; Their bird's nest is my purse. r F. G. thustulsvrownr.

THE TOWN ON THE HILL. We sighed, and sadly up the down Betook our way to the hill town; In our last walk, our last good-bye We just had said, we knew not why. We only thought it to be best To crush at once that small unrest, We knew not long unforged would be Love's chains—and we'd be fancy free. Then on the way we lightly jest 01 sighs and tears and hearts oppressed, Then pause awhile—that pause, ah, me! How dear in dreams and memory. In mine an unimpassidhed hand, The other an entwining band, Then with closed eyes that fear the bliss, A silent, short, dear sister's kiss. '''‘Good-bve," and neither heart did smart, Good-bye" and threw our hands apart. We knew not then upon the wold Our hands had scattered untold gold. Some day, perchance, the looks of youth Shall prove that they have more of truth, , And less of guile and more of good, Than all the words of womanhood. And we shall know that we were twain Some day, when looks and words are vain And lovetoo much and hold too dear What we neer prized that other year. Still on the town-crowned hill the lights Shall wavering shine through other nights, Still blow dark winds with fateful rhynsee, And chaugeful songs of olden times. Exvot. "Alas! for the tale that never is heard, Alas! for the thought that's never a wood, And the sighs that never become sweet tears, And the hearts Drat ache through the hopeless years.

Mr. Maurice Maurice Melrose went out calling the other even- ing, and after a brief stay took his departure, leaving his cane, by mistake, in the hall. He missed it in a few minutes, and came back after it, the young lady's• little sister meeting him at the door. " Ah, my little girl," he said, " weally I beg your pardon, don't you know, but I think I left a stick here." "I don't think you did, Mr. Melrose. I heard sister say so." " Aw, indeed, you flat- tab me; but how should your sister know? She did not see me go out; don't you know ?" "I don't know, sir, but I heard her say to Mr. Benton when you left, 'Well, that stick's gone at last.' That's all I know about it, Mr. Melrose." He didn't prosecute his inquiries any further.

SPRING FINDING TN BABARIA.—The Allgenzeine Zeitung gives some interesting particulars of remarkable success in indicating the presence of water springs on the part of a man named Beraz, who seems to be a recognised authority in such matters. The scene of his perfor- mances was in the Bavarian highlands, at a height of more than 1,300 ft. above the level of the sea. The corn- of Rothenberg, near Hirschorn, suffered greatly from want of water, and invited Beraz last autumn to endeavour to find some source of supply for them. He inspected the locality one afternoon in presence of the public authorities and a reporter of the Allgemeine Zeitung, and announced that water was to be found in certain spots at depths which he stated. The first spot was in the lower village, and he gave the likely depth at between 62ft. and 72ft., adding thatthe volume of water which the spring would give would be of about the diameter of an inch and a quarter. After incessant labour for four weeks, consisting mainly of rock blasting the workmen came on a copious spring of water at a depth of almost 67ft. What he declared about a water source for the upper village was very singular. He pointed to a spot where, he said, three water courses lay perpendicularly under one another, and running in parallel courses. The first would be found at a depth of between 22ift. and 26ft., of about the size of a wheaten straw, and running in the direction from south-east to north-west. The second lay about 42ft. deep, was of about the size of a thick quill, and ran in the same direc- tion; "The third, he said, lay at a depth of about 56ft., running sn the same direction, and as large as a man's Ettle finger. The actual results were as follows :—The first water-course was struck at a depth of 271 ft., running in the direction indicated, and having a diameter of one - fifth of an inch. The workmen came on the second at a depth of 42-2-3 ft ; it had a diameter of 7-25ths of an neh. The third was found at 62ift. below the surface, and having a diameter of 3-sths of an inch—all three running in the direction Beraz had indicated. Unfortunately no hint is given of his method of procedure. AxGwe min (patented). The Angels' Cake Is Mary Anderson's favourite. The attendance of members has been very good, considering ,all the meet- ings have to be held in the open air in the sandy. desert. A few of our brethren were in-the advance guard which .first reached Debbeh, and at night they retired to a remote point and opened -session in a sheltered corner, when they heard suspicious sounds beyond, found the slopes alive with stealthy fioudanese, gave the alarm, and averted a surprise assault. /We correspond with - .- 44,n Cameron •Highlar

In concluding-his -report, Visiting-Deputy Palmer says •:—"Taking the whole ',intc; consideration, I really believe that at the close of-this campaign our noble Order will have guod reason-to be proud of its members andtheir work during the long and arduous journey. AR members seam united together firmly, and determined to make the work of our Order a success. I only hope and pray that we may all be spared to return to our native land to reap the benefit of a few months' quietude, for which eve are allee anxiously yearning, after insielve months' campaign up the Nile.' _

This decline, it will be seen was recovered in 1884, and nearly £lOO,OOO be- sides. when the Chancellor of the Exchequer comes to balance his accounts for 1884 he will find that though nearly £900,000 more has been spent upon intoxicating tiquors, there has nevertheless about £280,000 less come into the Treasury by way of revenue therefrom. This Is due to the fact that while in 1884 there was an increase of expenditure upon beer of £2,047,912, as compared to 1.883, there was alongside ef it a decrease in the amount spent 04i spirit& and wise of £1,175,931; and as British spirits are taxed 10s. per gallon, foreign spirits 108. 4d. per gallon, and wine from Is. to 2s. per gallon, according to strength, while beer is only taxed 2 1-12 d. per gallon, we have the anomaly of a rising drink bill, with a fulling revenue therefrom. If we have regard te the fearful depreeeion whicla has prevailed in trade, and the bitter cries of destitution which have arisen frotniaearly every centre of industry throughout the country during the past year, and if we further take account •of the rapidly-growing sentiment against the use of intoxicating -liquors, -and also recog- nise the vastness and power of the agencies which hays been in operation combatting the drinking habits of the people, it will cause surprise and grief to thoughtful minds to find that, despite the powerful influences oper- ating in favour of sobriety, -the drink bill should yet have grown.- The fact supplies another illustration of the fearful potency of the legalised-temptations to drink which everywhere so extensively beset -the path of the people. Upon the moss lands between Southport and the Douglas there will be the same preference given to magnums for seed that is to be given in many other parts of Lancashire and Cheshire. Some farmers would prefer champions if they woqld fetch the same price. The lambing season in the open district near the mouth of the Douglas, on the west side, is late The calving season has been a very good one generally in the dairy district of Hesketh Bank, Becconsall, and Tarleton. In a herd of nearly 40 milch cows only one had picked the calf, and other dairy herds in the neighbourhood had done equally as well. In the district between the Douglas and Preston the lambing season is proceeding very satisfactorily, and there are many fine strong lambs which, with their dams, are doing well. There is agreat fall in the price of calving cows, and a farmer living on the west side of Preston writes to me that cows at their fourth and fifth calf are diffi- cult to sell at any price. He writes :—" I have bought a cow at second calf for 16 guineas which I could not have bought a year ago at less than 20 guineas." This fall in prices will affect a class of farmers who have fared pretty well during the last few years; on the other hand it will enable poor farmers to stock their land with more cattle. The appearance of wheat upon all sorts of land is highly satisfactory. The Cold has done it a great service in checking its growth at a time when a check was de- sirable. The area under wheat does not differ materially from that of last year. I find above the average quan- tity of hay in stacks, so that it cannot be the dread of dear hay which has brought down' the price of cattle. The artificial grasses in West Lancashire are looking in- variably well.

SHOCKING TRACTION ENGINE ACCIDENT.—On Tuesday morning, a little girl named Sarah Ann Brierley, aged IWO years, was crossing Ripponden-road, Oldham, when she was knocked down by a traction engine. The bind wheel passed over her from feet to head, killing her instantly. Her body was crushed to an unrecognisable mass. FEEDING THE UNEMPLOYED.—Baron F. De Rothschild gave a breakfast in Southwark on Tuesday morning, to 300 unemployed dock labourers. Princess Louise and Mrs Gladstone were present. Sir Stafford Northcote and Lord Rosebery wrote, urging emigration for the unemployed. Mrs Gladstone promised to give a similar breakfast. Tux WIGAN Tom; COUNCIL Ditsvons—The questions Involved in the resignation of Mr Ackerley, one of the town councillors of Wigan, came up before Justices Mathews and Smith, in the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday, when a rule absolute was made for a peremptory mandamus to is- sue, calling upon the Wigan Corporation to declare the seat held by Mr Ackerley to be vacant. DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.—On Monday night the foundry of Messrs A B Fraser and Co, in Regent-rd, Liverpool, was des- troyed by fire.—Late on Monday night,a fire occurred at Black- ' ford Bridge Printworks, belonging to Messrs Rumney and Co. A building twelve windows long, four wide, and two storeys high, was destroyed. DINNER TO SIR -GILBERT GREENALL.

-- In the Assembly Room of the Conservative Club, War- rington,on Saturday evening, a number of Conservative Workingmen gave a dinner to the candidate, Sir Gilbert Greenell, Bart. Mr John Robert, ecoupied the chair, and Mr William Heaton the vine-chair. There was a good attendance, and amongst those present were Sir Gilbert Greeiall, Bart, Mr Gi'bah Gireenall, the Rev S Wilkineou, Captain Reynolds, and Councillors Franoomb, W J Burgess, A Mackie, J B Wright, Sutton., Bolton, and Flatchinson. The dialler was provided by Mr Speakman, manager of the dab. Sabsequently toasts were drunk. Those of "The Queen" and "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family" were given from the chair with masioal honours, and "The health of the Bishops Clergy, and Ministers of all Deaeminations " was proposed by Mr W ft Abrahams and acknowledged by the Rev 8 Wilkinson, •Mr W Heaton replying to the toast of "The Army. Navy, and Anxiliary Forces" proposed by Councillor Franoomb. Mn 4 Tnonarretr, SENR. proposing "The Town and Trade of Warrington," said he thought there was only one present remedy to revive trade in Lancashire and Cheshire and other parts of the country, and that was the cutting of the Manchester Ship Cana. (Applause.) Cat the canal, and every man, wirman, and child, from the prince to the peasant would be benefited. He hoped they should ones mere see Sir Gilbert °Toenail in the House of Commons, and thought the time was drawing near when they would h.vir I. put shoulder to shoulder and return him. (Ap- plause). Mr B. Isanstwoon, in responding, referred to the benefit of promoting amicable relations between employers and employed, entreated Conservatives to work at the nest elec- tion shoulder te shonlder, and not ia a hollow' but in a stolid -square, to send the man of their choice to Parliament. He remarked that the working classes were the lever of every eleotton, and if they returned Sir Gilbert Greenall no doubt they woold get an inquiry into bad trade. They all suffered from it and if the remedy was in their own hands why not he determined ti use it. (Applause). Councillor MAXICIII also reeronded. He said that hav- ing been speeially invited to attend he could not for a mo- ment hesitate, if only to show that his affection for the greet of the evening had not cooled. They biped that Sir Gilbert would again be returned. They should be rejoined if it was only fora year, and if at the end of a year ha were to get tired and want to go home to the joys of Walton Hall they must oonsent. (Applause.) The speaker then re- ferred to Imperial and local matters.

WINDLE Scrroom v. GOLHORNE (2nd.)—Thls match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and resul- ted in a victory for the home team by four goals to three. NICHOL LANE V. HAYDOCK RECREATION.—IIayed on Saturday on the ground of the former, and a bard fought game resulted in a win for Nichol Lane by one goal to nil. ST HELENS. RECREATION V. LElGH.—These clubs met for the first time this season on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and after a very fast game resulted in a draw, a try each being scored. NEWTON V. FAIRFIELD.—PIayed on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a very pleasant game Newton were bailed the victors by one goal aid two minor points to nil. Egan, jun. scored the try, and S Rimmer sue- oeeded in adding the major point from a very difficult place.
vited to be present that 47enhag, but be (the speaker) had not had the .honour ef an invitAtion. He understood that

—no one was to be invited but the guest of the evening, and having got a ticket, was present as a working-man. They had heard it said that there was not such a thing as a Con- servative working-map, but there they had as lolly and as good a lot of working-men as ever he had seen, who gave a dinner to the man whom they wished should represent them. Sir Gilbert would be glad if he could return the compliment, but if be did he would be called a corrupt man. " But," tbe speaker continued, " let me say this ; this is one of the meetings that we have held before the event, but wll have a dinner after the event." (Applause.) He then asked, among other questions, was it true that the youngest alderman voted at the South-West Ward election, after what he said at the time of his election, and did the Radical cau- cus of Warrington believe that they were exalting the soCial status of women by obtaining their services as can- vassers at a political election ? The CHAIRMLN proposed "Health and prosperity to Sir Gilbert tireenall, Lady Greene'', and family," and sub- mitted the following resolution :—"That we, the working- men comprising this meeting, feel highly honoured at the presence of Sir Gilbert Greenall as our guest, and are much gratified to learn that he has consented to come for- ward as the Conservative candidate to represent this borough in Parliament ; and each Man present pledges himself to do his utmost by every legitimate means in his power to seenre his triumphant return." (Applause.) They would, be said, remember that some mouths ago Sit Gilbert Greenall was about to resign his position as candi- date for Warrington in the Conservative interest. What his reason was he could not understand, except that several of the Conservative party were of opinion that Sir -Gilbert had no chance of winning the borough again. But they, the workingmen, declined to accept that resignation, and induced their candidate to withdraw it. (Applause.)—The resolution having been carried, Sir Gleaner GILIIIINALL, in replying, said: Mr. Roberts and gentlemen,—l do not believe that a man can exist whose health has been proposed and received in so kind a manner and not be moved. (Hear.) There is a difficulty, gentlemee, in my suitably thanking you. Ido value, and I do appreciatli, th e very, very kind manner in which you have accepted the toast—(hear, hear, and a voice : You're welcome )—and the good wishes of my old and esteemed friend, Mr John Roberts. Hs has spoken of me most favourably and most kindly. lam inclined to think—nay, I am sure—that his friendship and and affectionate feelings towards me have made him speak too strongly and too favourably. (Hear, hear.) But, Mr Roberts, I thank you. I tbank you from the bottom of my heart for what you have said. I thank you all, gentlemen, all and each—(a voice: "Bleed him.")—in the same terms and in the same manner. (Applause.) There are occasion% and this is a pleasant occasion, when lam not able to lind words to ex- press to you all that I ought to say now. Gentlemen, this lean exceptional occasion. (Hear.) I think you have dons 1 something which I certainly never beard of before. You, my esteemed friends, working-men, have met me upon this occasion. lam here as your guest. I thank you heartily for the compliment, and I am proud to be with you. (Hear, hear) And now, gentlemen, I do not think there is either time or opportunity for me to enter upon political questions. I will try te bring matters into the closest possible compass. I will speak of the Government which we have. I say we have a vaccinating and unsatisfactory Government. (Hear, hear.) They are wrong in Europe, they are wrong in Asia. (A Voice : "All over the world.") They are floating very unsatisfactorily upon agitated waves in America and in Africa. What of Africa ? They are altogether without excuse. They have brought down this grand country to a degree of insecurity. They have separated this country from the great communities which Government held. They do not appear to me to have any—{a Voice : " Policy at all.") They do not appear to me to have any policy at all— (applause) except one, and that is to hold to office. (Renewed applause, and a Voice : " That's good.'') Now, what I desire, and I long to see to be gained, is when the present Government ceaees. And now, one word or two for myself. I do stand before you as your candidate. (Applause.) I depend upon the loyalty and attachment of the working-men. I am perfectly confident that when our battle is fought—and it will be fought, as I believe, by all of us unitedly-that we shall win-(applause)-and lam satisfied that the honour and the triumph of that victory will be from the courage, the unity, and the exertions of the work- ing classes. (Hear, hear.) It is perfectly true what my friend said, that I expressed myself willing again to be a can- didate for the representation°, the borough.(Applause.)When I expressed myself willing again to be a candidate for the re- presentation of the borough, I said emphatically and mar- kedly that I would only consent to stand as your candidate if I had from the working-men the expression of the work- ing-men's wish that I should stand, and if I found that I received it, that is the idea upon which I make my condi- tions in coming forward. But we have much to think of. We have much to do. We must take care to strap on our harness. We must not go unequipped into a content. Every man must work as if the result depended upon his own exertions—(applause)—and every man must feel that in fighting the battle he is nat merely fighting for Gilbert Greenall—(A Voice: "Sir Gilbert ")—but that he was really fighting to maintain the institutions of this country—(hear, hear)—that he was fighting mainly for the common good.of the country in which he lives. (Applause.) Now, gentlemen, do not let us forget for one moment that we intend to win. (Hear, hear.) I shall be with you. I shall be amongst you. I will do everything that I think is in my power and my duty, and lam sure I shall not say too strong words when I say ;his, that when we fight I shall be disappointed if I do not feel that everyone and each of you is trying to do his beet. Sir Gilbert then repeated that he thanked the workingmen for their cordial, loyal, and affec- tionate reception. (Applause.) Other toasts were given, and a resolution censuring the policy of the present Government was passed on the proposi- tion of Mr. Joule BITRUBSS, seconded by Councillor Bunoess.—Mr. G. Cropper and other gentlemen sang songs during the evening, Mr. G. Riley acting as accompanist. The proceedings terminated shortly before eleven.

EARLEsrows Swivrs team of players under the name if " Swift" met the second eleven of the Barlestown club OR the ground of the latter at Wargrave Moss, on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of a fair number of spectators. The Swifts are composed principally of well-known Rugby players connected with the Vulcan club, and, as could only be expected, they met wide') a defeat The home team had clatters pretty much their own way, and wen by ten goals to two. , RUNCORN" OLD BOYS V. WIDNES VICTORIA (L TEAM). —This retarn fixture took place on the ground of the latter on Saturday. Being the only match played in Widnes on that day, the Victoria Club did not fail to procure the ser- vices of some good players of the disengaged teams of the neighbourhood. Despite this circumstance, however, the visitors came off the winners, which spoke well for the able manner in which they combated their opoonenta. At the close of the game the score stood as follows :—Old Boys : 1 goal, 2 tries, and 3 minor points, to the borne team 1 goal, 1 try, and 3 minor points. The tries of the Old Boys were obtained by Abrams, Prince, and a substitute. lhe one obtained by Prince resulted in a goal, which was nicely kicked by Wishlade.

RIINCO'RN V. WALEDEN.—PIayed at Rencorn on Satur- day, when a most desultory game ended in a draw, the score being—Runcorn, 1 try and 1 minor point, to Walkden 1 try and 3 minor points. During the first half of the game II Hughes snored for Runcorn, and Prescott for Welkelen. In the latter portion of the game nothing but minor points were gained by either side, and what might have been a good genie was completely spoiled by the most frequent appeals of the Walkden players to the referee on the most frivolous points, thus staying all attempts at fast play. Teams : Runcorn : Woods, back; W Hughes, II Speakman, and F Johnson, three quarter backs; Ii Hughes and H An. drews, half baeks ; W Wright, W Mason, R Roberts, F Clarke, J Lewis, J Dean, J Barns, J Gatlev, and W Cox, forwards. Walkden : Grundy, back; Isherwood, Yates, and March, three-quarter backs ; Harper and Cook, half backs ; Grundy, Prescott, Urmson, Welsby, Jones, Rush- ton, B:mister, Barns, and Owen, forwards. WARRINGTON CRICICRT V.IFOOTRALL CLUBS.—This match was played on Saturday, on the Cricketers' ground. The Cricketers' captain won the toss and elected to play with the wind in his favour. The ball was set in motion and the Cricketers were soon thrown on the defensive. '1 he Warrington team were likewise returned the compliment, but the play in the first half was very evenly contested, and by the time for change of ends no goal had been obtained on either side. After a few minutes' grace the ball was again set in motion by the Cricketers' centre. Warrington, this time with the wind in their favenr, soon got the ball into the Cricketers' quarters, but owing to the good play of their backs it was quickly returned and the Warrington goal was sometimes in danger, but the steady play of Davies and Woodwood at back frustrated all attempts at scoring. The game still went on pretty evenly for about 15 minutes, when the Cricketer& showed signs of weakness and were again thrown on the defensive for a considerable length of time, the Warrington goal keeper and backs at this time being In mid-field. Several corner kicks fell to the War- rington team, but their efforts to utiliz.3 them failed on ac- count of the good defensive play of the Cricketers. The Warrington team continued to press the Cricketers for some time, but just before the game was at an end the Cricketers seemed to play more together, and by a combined rush the ball was driven into the Warrington quarters. Things began to look serious, bat time was called, and thus the game was brought to a conclusion, no goals being scored by either side.

_ EARLESTOWN V. NORTHWICH VICTORIA. DEFEAT OF THE LIVERPOOL CIIPHOLDERS. Some consternation was occasioned in Earlestown on Saturday night by a rumour that the Earlestown first team had been defeated by North- wlch Victoria by no less than 12 goals, in addition to three or four others disputed, to nil. The report was strongly discredited, but it has turned out a fact that Earlestown were defeated to that extent. The Victorians are the hold- ers of the Cheshire CLallenge Cup, and were represented by , their full strength as follows :—Goal, E Harper ; backs,. E Molyneux and J Rose; half backs, W H Hughes and G Vernon; forwards, T Mulkey, E Denton, E Turnbull, J Ma'am, Cr Plant, 1' Lever. To oppose this strong or- ganisation but ten players of the Earlestown Club journeyed to Northwich, and they had absent from their ranks no less than four of the first team—namely, J Duxhury, J Ellison, W Rich, and J Ogden. Second team men went in their places, but the match throughout was very one-eided. The Earlestonians took up the most unsatisfactory position in the field, the two backs (R Green and J Green) playing among the forwards, while Dagnall and Sims (centre and left wing respectively) played as the backs. Bowker (half back) took his position as goalkeeper, and Appleton (the or- dinary goalkeeper) played on the right wing. Toe three second eleven players, T Ferguson, W Murray, and J Gray, played anywhere where they could; as also did the captain (J Whalley). As was to be expected, the Cheshire cupholders almost did as they liked with their opponents, and before half time scored four goals. In the second half the ten Earlestown men were still more disorganised, and Dagnall, Sims, and Gray also tried their handl at goalkeep- ing. When time was called, the match—if it can be so called—resulted in a victory for Northivich by 12 goals to none. Never before in the history of the club has 12 goals been scored against the representatives of the Earleatown Club in one match. In concluding a report of the match a Northwich paper stated "After Northwich had scored two goals the vieitors made the game into a laughable farce, and acted more like clown football players than a team try- ing to sustain a fair reputation." WARettworosr V. Weruerrar (14).—Tbese clubs met to play off their return fixture on Saturday, at Latchford. The visitors only mustered 13 players, and this was in- creased by enlisting the services of Ashurst, of the Warring- ton second. Fitton had the selection of goals, and he chose the first, near the entrance, the wind in their favour. Davies kicked off, and a quicklollow-up was aided by Briggs mull- ing the ball, therefore no return was made. The first pack formed near the stand, whence Werneth forwards worked the leather into Warrington territory. Jolley, on the alert, got away a few yards' then was forced into touch. Forward play continued to be frequent, and credit is due to Werneth for their vigorous play, keeping the leather very close and quickly preventing Jolley and Warren feeding Barnes, and thus spoiling the Warrington back division of excellent chances. This kind of play ruled throughout the first half, and at half-time not even a minor was recorded to either team. Resuming, in the remaining portion of the game Warrington were assisted with a slight breeze. Barnes returned the kick off, and the locale of play was in the vie- itors' 25. Davies here made a strong rush, and just as he reached the goal line Greenwood pushed him into touch-in- goal. Many determined efforts then were put forth, but do all they would the Warringtonians could not register any winning point. A neat drop from the foot of Massey almost accomplished the desired purpose. Some neat passing be- tween Warren and Mtesey ended in the last-named player crossing the Werneth line after a really brilliant run. No improvement came from the place by Walsh. A serious mistake then cost Werneth a further try, owing to Green- wood missing the leather, and before he recovered himself Hayes had touched down. Runes kicked the goal. When I the game concluded Warrington were victorious by 1 goal, 1 try, and 6 minors to nil. Teams—Warrington : Walsh beck; Massey, Barnes, and Speakman, th:ee-quarters ; Jolley and Warren, half backs ' • Ashton (captain), F Tur- ner, Rigby, Dillon, Davies. Humphries, Povey, Hayes and F R Turner, forwards. Werneth : T Fitton (captain), back ; Briggs, Greenwood, and Spence, three-quarters ; Heath and Jinks, half backs ; F Eaton, Waller, Short- ridge, Bottomley, Nield, Ashurst, Brierlev, and Thompson, forwards.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

• The fine weetiier of the past few days basesabled us to get ,in some early potatoes which were rather ad- vanced' in growth, and much care had to be ezereised notto injure thesprouts. -We prefer to dig and plant as we proceed, and in this instancewe introduced a little dry half-decayed manureunderneath the sets, as well as a little on the top. 14c, kind of potatoes should be planted nearer than le inches between the rows, and 8 inches between the sets. A small planting of lettuee was also made 61n, from plant to plant, and Bin. between the rows, with the view of drawing out every other plant as soon as they attain useable size. Drills were drawn for pees 4in. deep and sft. distant. Before the seeds were soWn they were placed in a flower-pot, and water poured over them, one of the fingers being held on the hole at the bottom till the peas were covered over, when it was withdrawn sufficiently to allow the water to run out. The peas are then put in another vessel, and a pinch orl two of red lead sprinkled ever them, and the whole, shaken UD and down till every pea is covered with the' lead. They may then be sown, id are considered per- fm.Py safe from the attacks of mice. If the peas are saterated with paraffin they are said to be equally secure. Considering the little labour and expense volved in the application of either of these preventives, we strongly advise that one or the other should be adopted. , Broad beans should not be sown nearer than 4f.t.1 from row to row, and the further •tisey, as well as the pea rows, are from each other in cottage gardens, the. better they and the other crops will suoeeed. Par- snips are sown in drills about 2in. deep and /Gin, distant, in which the seeds may be thinly scattered, or they may be deposited in patches Bin. apart, to be finally reduced to one plant. We managed to catch the surface of the 'soil sufficiently dry to be trod regularly on over by a shuffling of the feet. The ground was then raked, and the drills drawn. The onion plot is prepared similarly to that for parsnips as to treading and raking, and the seeds are best sown in very shallow drills six or eight inches distant, which we consider far preferable to the old- fashioned method of sowing broadcast in beds, inasmuch as it admits of the hoe passing through them, so as to destroy the weeds, and if between every sixth row the 1 space of one foot is left, the operator can stand in that and hoe or hand-weed without making a footprint be- tween the rows. Some entertain the idea that more onions can be got by sowing broadcast, but this is not the case, as they can be left any thickness in the rows, I and if these are 6in. distant there is really no space wasted, and the crop is much more regular than it can be by the broadcast system of sowing. TILE FRONT GARDEN.—This, like every other depart- ment of gardening, is now increasing daily in interest by the appearance of one cherished treasure after another ' through the soil, and as most have so far advanced, the 'borders or beds may be slightly forked over so as to give the whole a neat appearance. From this date most things of a hardy nature may be transplanted except bulbous plants, which resent any interference with their roots during their growing season. Plants of weak growth should be moved from the immediate shade of vigorous plants, which impoverish the soil to such an extent that weak subjects cannot exist.: It is a good plan, where plants are being moved, to make a little pre- paration by taking out a spadeful or two of soil more than is needful to make room for the plant and replace it ' with well decayed manure or rich soil from the vegetable garden. Roses trained against the wall of the dwelling may now be pruned by moving all of weakly growth and shortening others. Some varieties make over a yard of growth in the season, a third of which may be cut away unless the plants are very vigorous indeed; then only, the weak ends need be removed. See that all are made secure to the wall with shreds and nails if there are no wires stretched on the wall for the purpose. Nails may also be driven in the wall and the shoots attached to them with pieces of string. THE WlNDOW.—Geraniums that are usually designated Pelargoniums will require more root room. Whether they are plants that have been cut back in the autunin and treated according to directions given at the time, or those put in as cuttings during the past year, they will all need attention. The fresh pot should be washed in- side and out, and should be sufficiently large to allow an inch of fresh soil all round the roots. The pots should be thoroughly dtained by placing an oyster shell or a concave piece of crock on the bottom of the pot so as to well cover the hole. On this about two inches of broken crocks should be placed, and these should be covered with half decayed leaves or the rougher portion of soil intended for potting. By this arrangement the smaller particles of the soil are prevented from mixing with the crocks and obstructing the free passage of water. Those who disregard this rule will at some time or other dis- cover their plants water-logged, when they will assume a yellow, sickly hue, and finally succumb.

THE DYNAMITE OUTRAGES IN Lowncrc—At London, on Monday, James G Cunning¢am and Henry Burton were a- gain charged with high treason and felony in connection with the dynamite outrages at tbe tower and elsswhere. No

further evidence was preierrel against them, and they were remanded till Friday. Both prisoners presented ttn appear- ance of intense weariness, and walkcd in and out of the court in a listless fashion. The two detectives who were despatched to America to ascertain the antecedents and con- nections of the two men charged with the London dynamite outrages, have returned, having obtained some important in- formation concerning the accused.

ANTI-VACCINATION DEMONSTRATION AT LEICESTER.— One of the largest demonstrations ever held in Leicester took place on Monday to protest against the enforcement of the Vaccination Acts against 5,000 defaulters. The people met in the Market place, where, it is stated over 20,000 per- eons assembled. Several hundreds of banners were sent by sympathisers in various parts of the country. The "friends" in Belgium forwarded a banner with the incription in French "Neither fines nor imprisonment will preventi vaccine from being a poison, nor the vaccination laws an infamy." There was also a horse and a cow drawn in vans as sources of vac- cination, and an open bier with a coffin as the result. A large detachment of men who had been imprisoned headed the procession, followed by a larger number whose goods had been seized and sold oy public auction. On returning to the Market-place copies of the Acts were fastened to iron bars and burned amid the yells of the crowd. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Another fruitless attempt has been made to settle the question of professionalism in football. The annual March meeting of the Association took place on Monday evening, when the representatives of the Northern clubs did thvir beet to effect a settlement, but were defeated, being 11 short of the required majority of two-thirds required to make an alteration of the rules of the Association. This shows a decided advance to professionalism since the meeting on the 19th January, when the number Of voters required to carry the proposal was 35. This is a step in the right direction, but still the question has already been awaiting settlement too long, and threatens, if not closed speedily, to do more harm to the game than the would-be amateurs seem to think.

DARING GAROTTE BOBBER2.—At Sheffield, on Monday night, whilst Mr Ball, solicitor, was proceeding home, two men walked beside him. Suddenly they lifted him off his feet, carried him into an entry, and while one held him by the throat the other robbed him of money and valuable papers. He was then struck with a life preserver, and left unconscious. He lies in a dangerous condition. &norm, THURSDAY Noux.—The reinforcements sent from here yesterday reached lid`Neill's &Juba with but little op- position, and no casualties occurred. The whole of M'Neill's forces are now concentrated, and skirmishers have been sent out to clear the bush of Osman Digna's fol- lowers. &TARIM, THURSDAY, 1-20 P.3l.—Tbe Grenadier Guards, the Shropshire and the Surrey ItAgiments, and two bat. talons of Indian troops, started at seven o'clock this morning to escort the convoy to the zereba on the. Tamai road. OFFER OF 5,060 KAFFIRS FOR THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.

In Natal some member l of the Shepstone family have offered to raise a corps of 5,000 Kaffir for service in the Soudan. It has also been proposed to enlist a force of young Boers for the same purpose. NEWS FROM KORTI. KORTI, SllNDAY.—Another spy has returned from Khar- I toum. He reports that the Mandi is still at Omdurman.

The fire which was con- fined to five tar stills, was got under in about an hour. A man named William Summer, employed on the premises, was burnt to death. ,

THE EXAMINER'. SATURD A Y. MARCH 28, 1885.
MAP OF THE SEAT OF WAR.

The commander of the forces at Metemmah sent to the Mandi, ou the retirement of the English from Gobat to ask for instructidna. He was ordered to go to Berber with his forces. There is much trouble with the Arabs in the west, the greater part of whom have now declared against the Mandi. The report that General Gordon killed three Arabs before he was speared is confirmed by the spy just arrived. Ho says that the General emptied all the barrels of his revolver into his assailants before he fell. The Mandi has sentenced many natlies to death for not having revealed the hidden treasures Which he believed existed. Owing to a large capture of slaves at Khartoum, many women have been brought by the slave dealers into the neighbourhood of this place, and disposed of to the natives at the rate of 100 dollars each.

KORTI, MONDAY.—A deserter from Berber brings in the news that orders have been received from the Ma.di that all the troops there shall go at once to Khartoum, and that the natives of Berber and the neighbourhood are to advance without delay against the English. Lord Wolse- ley reviewed the 19th Hussars to-day, and afterwards ad- dressed them, warmly praising both officers and men for their services.

Canto, MONDAY.—Lord Wolseley, accompanied by his staff, will leave to-morrow for Congola, to which place Prince Hassan will in ftll probability proceed. It is stated that a Chicago firm has received an order for 5,000 000 cans of meat for the British army in Egypt. Messrs Andrew and Tames Stuart, tube manufacturers, Coatbridge, have received a Government order for the manu- facture of fifty miles of water-pipes for the line to be laid between Suakim and Berber.

A Parliamentary return issued en Saturday shows that the casualties in the force which marched from Korti for Metammeh, up to January 23, were 95 killed, 184 wounded, and 42 admitted to hospital. At Abu Klea, January 17th, there were 74 killed and 79 wounded ; and in the actions of the 19th and 21st January there were 21 killed and 105 wounded. The total number of casualties to the whole Nile Expeditionary force from the let September was-147 officers and 4,100 men sick ; 16 officers and 240 men died from all causes; 19 officers and 165 men admitted to hos- pital for wounds; 10 officers 85 men killed in action : 13 men died from wounds, and 1 officer and 3 men were drowned.

div.head: ZEBEFIR PASHA.
div.p: ZEBEFIR PASHA.

MALTA, SATURDAY.—Her Majesty's deepatch vessel Iris has arrived here from Alexandria, having on board Zebehr Pasha, his two sons, and nephew. She will continue her voyage to-day. Her destination has not transpired.

THE COLONIAL CONTINGENT. SYDNEY, WEDINTESDAY.—The address to the Governor ap- proving the action of the New South Wales Government in depatehing a contingent to the Soudan has been carried unanimously In the Legislative Council. In the Legislative Assembly it was carriad by 63 votes to 24. The debate was marked by great enthusiasm. and at the close loud cheers were given for the Queen.
ATTACK ON ANOTHER CONVOY. DESPATCH FROM SIR GERALD GRAHAM.
The following telegram has been sent by Lieutenant- General Sir G Graham to Lord Wolseley, dated Suakin, 25th March, 12-45 a.m.:—

"This morning (2 yesterday) sent out convoy to M'Neill's aireba with escort 15th Sikhs, 28th Bombay and Madras Sappers. At three miles distant convoy halted, as ordered,• commenced cutting road and formed zareba. A battalion of Guards and Marines from M'Neill's marched towards them, and were attacked on the way by long-range fire, Lieutenant Merchant (Marines) and one private being wounied. About 2-0 p.m. the escorts met when Guards and Marines took over convoy, giving over two wounded to return to Suakim. Returning to zareba, Guards and Marines were attacked twice. No complete report vet received from M'Neill. Cavalry escort accompanied convoy, consisting of one squadron Bengal Lancers, one squadron 20th Hussars. 'rivalry behaved very well when square was attacked, keeping clear of infantry fire and checking enemy's advance by volleys from dismounted men. Guards and Marinee showed great steadiness under fire. Cavalry escort and Native Infantry returned to buskin). Casualties as re- ported were: Killed, Coldstreams, one private ; wounded, Captain Dalrymple, eight men. Marines, five men. Nomi- nal rolls to-morrow." Suatrix, WEDNESDAY NooK—Another convoy escorted by Indian troops, left the camp this morning for the zareba on the Tamai road. A captive balloon is floating over the convoy in order to observe the movements of the enemy. The Grenadier Guards have started to bring back the Sur- rey Regiment from the Hasheen zareba. The head-quar- ters clamp was moved to-day to a point two miles nearer to Tenni.

SHAME, WEDNESDAY, 8-50 P.M.—The Grf nadier Guards have returned here with the Fast Surrey Regiment from the liasheen samba. During the march a few shots were ex- changed with the enemy, bat there were no cassalties on the British side. The convoy which left this morning for the nareba on the Tamai road returned here this evening with- out being attacked. This afternoon the Guards moved to fresh camping ground near Tamai. The enemy's loss in yesterday's skirmish is estimated at 403. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—TWO Soudanese shiekhs have left for Constantinople in order to enter the Sultan's service. CAlso, WEDNESDAY—The second battalion of the Ox- fordshire Light infantry Regiment, from Gibraltar, arrived to -day. JEDDAH, ltrESDAY.—lntelligence from Yemen reports the province to be perfectly tranquil. The Mandi's proclama- tions had made no impression upon the population. ANOTHER ATTACK ON A CONVOY.

Sir Gerald Graham reports that another convoy was attacked on Thursday on the Tamai road. The Arabs, despite the great losses they have suffered, exhibited their usual bravery, and many ot them fell within a few yards of the square. Oar loss was very slight. A report which was current on Wednesday to the effect that Osman Digma had made overtures for peace is declared to be absolutely co- founded.

ZAREBA ON THE WAY TO TAMAI,THURSDAY.—The convoy which started from Buakim at seven o'clock this morning arrived here safely this afternoon. A small force of the rebels attacked the convoy, but were repulsed all round with considerable loss, about a hundred of the enemy being killed. On the British side there were three wounded. The rebels attacked with the greatest bravery, advancing singly within 20 yards of the square. TUESDAY'S FIGHTING.-GREAT SLAUGHTER.

The Daily News cgrrespondent at Suakim writes :—Tne gallant manner in which the Celdstreams and Marines fought the enemy on Tuesday against enormous odds deserves the greatest praise. The Arabs charged the square time after time in thousands. It was of no avail. They never arrived within ten yards, but were mowed down by our withering fire, hundreds falling at a time. Their loss .must have been enormaus, but, owing to the thickness of the bush', it is impossible to give an estimate of it. Their silence only proves their discomfiture. GENERAL GRAHAM'S BALLOON.

Major Tempter's captive balloon floats over the zarebas. The balloon is secured by two ropes. Messages pass up and down one of the ropes to and from the officer in the car of the balloon. Had it been in the air above the zarebas oa Sunday the surprise and heavy loss would have been avoided. The bush is so dense that even a mounted man cannot see bodies of men crawling towards him until they are within twenty paces. From the altitude of the balloon, however, the observer will ba able to look down between
the bushes, and conldat once detect persons moving among thene.—Standard.

div.head: MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN.
div.p: MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN.

Sol:mum, THURSDAY, 10-50 A 111.—The—Qtteen has tele- graphed to General Graham, through Sir Henry Ponsonby, expressing her great admiration of the conduct of her troops, for whose welfare she feels very anxious. Especial mention le made in the telegram of Her Majesty's admira- tion of the gallant and untiring perseverance displayed by her troops under the most trying and harassing warfare in which they could be engaged.

div.head: MANCHESTER SIIIP CANAL
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SIIIP CANAL
FRIDAY.

Mr Pember, the leading counsel for the promoters, an- nounced that he expected soon to conclude the engineering evidence in favour of the scheme, and he wished to know what the Committee intended to do with regard to calling on the opponents to proceed with their engineering evidence. —Mr Bidder, foethe Mersey Dock Board, and Mr. Pope, for the London and North-Western Railway Company, at first declined to comply with this suggestion, on the ground that their Case would be prejudiced if presented in halves, bet when the Chairman intimated that the Committee did not intend to give any decision on the engineering evidence un- less they should come to the conclusion that there were insuperable difficulties in the way of the canal, the opposi- tion to the engineering part of the evidence of the petition- ers being offered at the chse ef that for the promoters was withdrawn, and it was arranged that the engineers for the opponents should called as soon as those on the other side had been examined.—Mr Vernon Harcourt, civil engineer, who fast year gave evidence against the Bill, said that the channel now proposed would came no interference with the estuary of the Mersey.—Mr John Fowler, engineer to the Tees Conservancy Board, gave evidence to a like effect.— Mr Messent, engineer to the Tyne Commissioners; Mr Wheeler, engineer to the Boston Harbour Commissioners; and Mr J Dean, eogineer to the Clyde Navigation, who were also called, agreed in the opinion that no injurious effect, either en the bar at the mouth of the Mersey or on the estuary of the river, was to be anticipated from the works of the proposed canal. The erosion of the banks would be prevented, and to that extent the estuary would be benefited. —The Committee adjourned until Monday.

div.head: MONDAY.-A GREENIEN IS WITEI PETITIONERS.
div.p: MONDAY.-A GREENIEN IS WITEI PETITIONERS.
The Lords' Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill sat again on Monday, and took further engineering evi- dence.

Mr. ALFRED GILES, M.P., the engineer of the Southamp- ton Docks, who gave evidence in favour of the two former schemes, said his opinion with regard to them remained un- altered—that with low training walls, a deep-water channel might have been constructed through the estuary of the Mersey without any possible risk. Being an old marine surveyor and having taken a great many soundings, he did not admit the possibility of measuring the capacity of such an estuary as the Mersey within 2,000 000 or 3,000,000 yards. He could not conceive bow the channel could be coaxed from the Lancashire to the Cheshire side, to the detriment of Garston. Eastham was the best point that could have been Selected for the termination of the canal. He considered that the docks which the promo- ters intended to construct at Manchester, Warring- ton, and Partington were admirably adapted for carrying on a very large trade, and the sites were very well selected. As soon u ships passed the bar at Liver- pool they would make their way to the entrance to the canal, and during ordinary full tide they would ascend without locking. He gathered from the petition of the Mersey Dock Board that further dock extensions at Liverpool were con- templated, the increase in the trade at that port being at the rate of 4 per cent, per annum.—Cross-examined by Mr Bidder, for the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board: Be be- lieved Manchester and the neighbourhood was rich enough to find any amount of money, it the people wanted to carry out this great scheme—Will they be content to spend £lOOOOOOO and wait six or seven years More they get nay interest? They will not have to spend £10,000,000: £7,000,000 is quite enough. The £10,000,000 includes the purchase money of the Bridgewater Canal, sad that canal is a paying investment.—Would it be a paying investment side by side with the Ship Canal? You have over 2 000,000 tons of traffic OR the Bridgewater Canal, and nearly the same amount on the Weaver Navigation, and they will be very much better accommodated by the Ship Canal. • Mr. PEEIBEB informed the Committee that the promo- ters bad settled terms with several of the petitioners, viz., the Widnes Local Board, the traders of Widnes, St. Helens Corporation, the traders of St. Helens, the proprietors of the Hutchinson Dock at Widnes, Mr Grace (a landowner), Mr. Naylor (another landowner), the Trustees of the Weaver Navigation, and the proprietors of the Rochdale Canal. The Weaver Trustees had come to an agreement with the pro- moters on a basis perfectly satisfactory to both parties. As soon as the terms of the several agreements were drawn up mad printed, the promoters would be ready to lay them before the Committee, should their lordships so desire. Mr. F. E. Dtrrroisk engineer to the Mill wall Docks, gave evidence that the plans of the proposed canal and docks were well designed for carrying on a large trade. Mr. PEMBER then asked for the guidance of the Commit- tee upon the course of procedure. Having consulted with his colleagues. the CHAIRMAN announced that the Cimmittee had decided that everything connected with the estuary and the bar of the river Mersey must be kept separate from the rest of the case. With re- gard te minor engineering points, they might be taken at once or in connection with the commercial case. They would like to proceed with the rebutting evidence imme- diately the engineering evidence of the promoters was con- cluded. Mr. JOSEPH PEGG and Mr. H. HILL, pilots on the River Mersey, gave evidence that the channels in the river were due to the "freshets" coming down the river, aided by the ebb tide. _ _ .
This concluded the engineering evidence for the pro- nsoters.

Captain GRAH&M HILLS, marine surveyor to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, was the first witness called for the petitioners. Examined by Mr. Bidder who reserved his speech), the witness stated that the bar of the Mersey had always been in a critical state, being affected by _changes in the river, and any operation on the river affected the bar. The Committee adjourned before the emmination of wit- ness had been concluded.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Captain Grtaniat HILLS, marine surveyor to the Mersey Docks Board, was further examined for the opponents. He said the charts of the Mersey showed the channel about Gersten varied greatly, and the Eastham channel was some- times overlaid with sandbanks of considerable depth. There was only a given quantity of water for the use of the es- tuary,and any increase of depth at one point would decrease at another. Whenever the Garston channel was in better condition than usual, the Eastham channel was starved. The witness argued from these facts that any attempt as pro- posed to make a permanent channel from the entrance of the canal at Eastham to Bromborongh Pool, a distance of two miles. would be a serious mischief to the estuary. The en- closures of marsh lands during the past 00 years did not amount to more than 1,500 or 1,600 acres, instead of 13,000 acres as stated the previous day. The latter figure related to enclosures from the time of the dark ages. Questioned concerning Mr Lyster'e alternative plan for the construction of a ship canal along the Cheshire shore, witness stated he did not approve of the plan, and was not asked for his ad- vice upon it, being out of the country at the time. He saw a Manchester writer had threatened that if Liverpool peo- ple made such a fuss about the canal the promoters would abandon Liverpool and cut the cmal into the Dee. (Laughter.) That was the alternative plan be should ap- prove.—ln re-examination Captain Hills stated that, in his opinion! Mr Lystees plan was less objectionable than that

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
of the promoters. It followed the sinuosities cf the high- water line, and Cid not cut oft the indentaticas to the same

extent nor enterso far into the Weave-. WEDNESDAY. Mr-. Leader Williams was re-called, and explained upon a plan the nature of the embankment it was propos,d t) con- struct along the Cheshire shore, and the number of openings therein for the influx of the tide,. It was not the fact that he was going to make a continuous embankment all the way from Frodsham to Eastham.—By Mr. Bidder : Under the general powers of the bill he thought he had power, with the consent of the landowners, to deposit the spoil on their land, and so raise it above flood level. There would be a continuous roadway along the whole of the embankment, but it would not be a public road. The top of the embank- ment would be 9fl above high water. Mr. LYSTEE, engineer-in-chief to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, described the number of engineering works in which he had been engaged on the Mersey and other rivers. He had considered Mr. Leader Williams's plan, and to his judgment it presented many very great objections, indeed, many of the objections of last year. The scheme would tend to the silting up of the estuary.— He expressed an opinion last session to the effect that a canal could be carried down to the estuary without injuriously affecting the estuary. That was the alternative scheme which had been referred to.— Mr Bidder: Provided that Manchester should have a canal, you are of opinion that such a canal as you have de- a ised in your plan would be one that would be admitted? Most distinctly. I say that the riparian canal prepared by me would minimise the danger. I am quite open to fur- ther minimising that danger if necessary.—Da you think a canal to Manchester in itself desirable ? Certainly not. As a practical man, having great experience at Liverpool, I cannot but regard it as the most utopian idea.—The Chairman : What is the total difference in acreage between the two plans? Witness : Their total interference with the acreage of the estuary within the limits of deviation is 1,480 acres, as against 581 of mine. In my calculation I exclude the river Weaver, because I intended to let the tide in and out under the canal by means of syphon. In my plan I protect myself by my special clause, which says that any exclusion of tidal water muet be compensated for. I am quite prepared to say to your lordships that, if you think my plan projects too far into the estuary, I will shove it up further. (Laughter.) My plan simply wets its feet in the estuary ; yours is up to its neck. (Laughter.) I did not go into question where the compensaticn is to be made.

ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.—ENERGETIC PREPARA- TIONS IN INDIA. ALTAI:WAD, SUNDAY.—Orders were issued on Saturday to mobilise two army corps, aggregating 25,000 men, with two strong divieions in reserve. The intention is to throw 25 000 into Aeshin while the weather is cool for marching. General Roberts will probably command, with the Duke of Connaught and General Macpherson as Divisional Generals. The greatest enthusiasm prevails. Sikh recruits are coming forward in hundreds. Scindia has placed his army and the entire resource of his State at the disposal of the British, offering to lead his forces persenally. It is believed that England will send 15,000 men as a permanent increase of the Indian garrisons. The Pioneer says that Lord Dufferin's statesmanship is fully relied on by India. A MESHED), MARCH 17TEL—Outwardly all is quiet IhßerAell M , but an immediate Raseian advance en Herat is deemed highly probable. A concentration of Russian troops in this direction is reported. Measures for the defence ef Herat are being taken.—Tintcs. CALCUTTA, TUESDAY.—Orders will shortly be issued for the recall of the offic.re who are absent from their regiments on leave.

Catcurra, THURSDAY. —At a conference at Allahabad be- tween the Viceroy and the Cot/inlander-in-Chief it was re- solved to send 25,000 men to the Bolan Pass, under tbe command of General Roberts, while another force of the same strength will subs:quently advance upon Rawal Pin- dee. A reserve force of 10,000 men will be formed and placed under the command of the Duke of Connaught. Be- info cements to the number of 15,000 men are to be drawn from England.

Boranrv, Tnrinsnev.—The Dslre of Connaught's return to Europe has been indefinitely postponed. his Royal High. nose having obtained leave to stay in India. Should the negotiations between England and Russia on he Afghan boundary question fall through, Sir Donald Stewart, Com- mander-in-Chief in India, will take the command of the Quetta Division. The French transport Oise, the French steamer Argo, and the American barqne Sarah Hodart, were totally wrecked. Seventeen lives were lost. Tile; PRINCE OF WALES IN BRUSSELS. BRUSSELS, TIICHSDAY.—The Prince of Wales, aec)m- pamed by Prince Albert Victor, arrived here at half-past four o'clock this morning from Ge-many, their Royal High- nesses proceeding to the Royal Palace. REVOLT OF NATIVES IN CANADA. OTTAWA, MONDAY Ninwv. In the Canadian Perna- niSir John M'Donald, the Premier, announced that:n t a to-day,forceof half-breeds, estimated at 450, under the command of the well-known Louis Real, had revolted at Prince Albert, overcome the local authorities, and were new masters of the place. The rebels had oat the telegraph wires so that the authorities should have no knowledge of their proceedings, but it has transpired that the rebels have captured the loci I °lintels, and at present hold there as pri- soners. The news has created much excitement. Rein. forcements will in all probability be sent tip from Toronto Ito quell the revolt. Prince Albert is on the west /shore ef ' Lake Scum. near Port Percy. A loop-line railway runs close to the place. FIFTEEN POLICEMEN KILLED. OTTAWA, WEDWEsDAT.—The insurgent half-breeds in Manitoba are beaded by Loins Riel, who wa.s the leader of the rising which was suppressed by the expedition under Lord Wolseley in 1870. OTTAWA, WEDNESDAY Ene veNo.— The Dominion Gov- ernment has received noinformation of any engagement having occurred between the mounted police and the half- breeds under Louis Mel. The rising is confined to a small district near Fort Carlton, 000 miles north-west of Winni- peg and 400 miles north of the international boundary. Riel is reported to have 400 half-breeds with him. One of the acts of violence committed by him was the seizing of six settlers, binding them, and imprisoning them in a church. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.-A despatch from Winnipeg, published here, States that an engagement has taken place on the North Saskatchewan River between the mounted Police and the insurgents. Fifteen police are reported to have been killed. The rebel loss is unknown. A later edition of the New York Herald of to-day pub- lishes a despatch stating that an engagement has occurred at Fort Carlton, Manitoba, between the half-breeds, under Louis Riel, and the mounted police, in consequence of the refusal of the latter to surrender. Three Indian bands are stated to have joined the rebels, who now number 3,000 men. Troops are being sent from Winnipeg. It is mid that 40 whites are prisoners in the hands of the half-breeds.

The High Commissioner for Canada has received a telegram lion Sir J Macdonald stating that the accpants of the outbreak at Fort Carlton are exaggerated. It is not believed that any Indians will join the half.breeds.

WIDNES AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The deputation appointed by the Widnes Local Board with the object of endeavouring to obtain clauses for the protection of the district from the Manchester Ship Canal Company may be considered, speaking generally, to have succeeded in their object. The general clauses agreed upon include the following provisions :—One for the maintenance of the entrance to the docks, so as to prevent the entrances being silted up, so that vessels can always get to the deep bed of the river, and so obtain entrance to the Ship Canal. A clause for protecting the outfall of any watercourse or sewer within the district ; and if the same become prejudi- cially affected the Canal Company undertake to make them good to the satisfaction of an arbitrator. If at any time the river Mersey, by reason of the construction of the canal, becomes BO injured that vessels will be unable to be navi- gated in as free a manner as at present, vessels to and from Widnes will be entitled to use the canal free of tolls. A further clause provides that the company shall, to the reasonable satisfaction of the Local Board for the district, construct, provide, and maintain a communicttlon across the canal above Runcorn Br,dge by means of a ferry " or otherwise," for the conveyance of passengers, animals, car- riages, and goods in communicition with the ferry, the same to be as convenient as the communication at present existing. In case of any dispute, the matter is to be referred I to the Board of Trade.

Tao deceased was removing some furniture to Gresford, when the gun which he carried in his pocket exploded, bring downwards, and inflicting a large wound above the knee. H hailed a man near him, and assistance being procured th 3 wound was bound up, but the deceassd expired twenty minutes after the accident. A verdict of accidental death was returned. Can it be that he is strongly averse to women having votes, or does he think that those who possess them should show no interest in an election beyond putting themselves into the hands of Con- servative wire.pullers ? The CHAIRMAN, in proposing a resolution pledging the meeting to support Sir GILBERT GREENALL, let the cat out of the bag as to certain differences of opinion amongst the leaders of the Conservative party. It will be remembered that in August last we gave an account of a meeting of Conservatives held at the Lion Hotel, at which there was some- thing like a revolt against Sir GILBERT GREENALL, and at which (in ludicrous igno- rance of his being a Liberal) Mr. DANIEL ADAMSON was spoken of as a more likely candidate. The statement we published was contradicted, md it was added that the Conservative party were united in sup- port of Sir GILBERT. This was taken at the time for what it was worth, and that it was not worth much may be gathered from the following extract from the speech of Mr. JOHN ROBERTS, who presided at the dinner on Saturday: "They would," he said, "remember that some months ago Sir GIL- BERT GREENALL was about to' resign his position as candidate for Warrington in the Conservative interest. What his reason was he could never understand, except that several of the Conservative party were of opinion that Sir GILBERT had no chance of winning the borough again." We thank Mr. ROBERTS for thus blurting out the truth as to this bit of local history, for that it is the truth cannot now be doubted, after all that has happened. It must be very pleasant for the "odd, old fellow" to have dinned in his ears publicly what he has most probably heard often enough privately, namely, that there are several of his own party who agree with the Liberals in thinking that he has "no chance of winning the borough again." But, like Macbeth, he is determined to die with har- ness on his back; he may be in the way, but he is not going to step aside to please those who may be "waiting for dead men's shoes." If Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT is waiting, he will let him wait. The " Old Obediah" is in the field, and he does not mean to retire in favour of the "Young Obediah "—until he is beaten. This much may be inferred from the reply which Sir GILBERT made to the gushing speeches that were showered upon him. Un- fortunately, little else wa,s to be gathered from his reply. He was, of course, saponaceous as ever, and that is saying a great deal. Equally, of course, he "did not think there was time or opportunity for him to enter upon political questions." 'Tis ever, thus. Why do they not give him a night to himself? Denied time and opportunity a$ he hat been all these years, his soul must by this be on th, eve of bursting for deliverance. He did venture to say, whilst trying to " bring mat- ters into the closest possible compass," that the Government were" floating very unsatis- factorily upon agitated waves in America and in Africa ;" but nobody seemed to know what he meant. It may be that he regards the Afghans as a tribe of American Indians. It would certainly not be more singular than his having become oblivious of having voted against working-men in the counties having votes, or in favour of the retention of flogging in the Army. "Bless him," as the "jolly lot' said at the dinner on Saturday. At his time of life it is out place for him to become " a fisher of men "—he would be better employed in angling for the small fry in Walton reser- voir.

THE Ship Canal Inquiry before the Lords' Committee is again in full swing. It is much to be regretted that arrangements could not be made for dealing with the matter by a Joint Committee of both Houses of Parlia- ment; for, apart from the great cost of the inquiries, the risk is again incurred of the whole proceedings being nullified by con- flicting decisians. It is a scandal upon the Legislature that such a thing should be pos- sible; and when we have got rid of a few biz, burning questions, the evil will have to be remedied. It is satisfactory to see that there is a disposition on the part of their lordships to avoid an undue prolongation of the inquiry, thus saving their own time, and the time and money of the promoters. The opposition, too, is less formidable than it was when proceedings commenced. On Monday, Mr. PEMBER, on behalf of the pro- moters, was in a position to announce that terms had been settled with several of the petitioners against the Bill, including the Widnes Local Board and traders of Widnes, the Corporation and traders of St. Helens, the proprietors of the Hut- chinson Dock at Widnes, the trustees of the Weaver Navigation, and the proprie- tors of the Rochdale Canal. Warrington, as our readers are aware, is joined with the promoters by virtue of a rate in sup- port of the Bill of twopence in the pound. The opposing counsel seem to think that Warrington has made good terms, particu- larly when the fact is taken into account that, if the scheme is carried out, there will be a dock of zz acres at Arpley Meadows. It is each for himself in this as in other matters, according to the way of the world ; and there can be no question that the pros- pect of money flowing into Warrington during, the construction of this 22 acre dock has had much to do with stimulating the en- thusiasm of the inhabitants in favour of the Bill. According to the estimates prepared by Mr. ABERNE-Tny and Mr. LEADER WILLIAMS, the dock at Warrington will cost £95,084, which means in the usual order of things an expenditure of something over £lOO,OOO. In addition there will of course be the cost of construction of the canal east and west of the docks, so that it is impossible for the scheme to be carried out without, giving an impetus to the trade of the district. The people of Warrington in throwing out their bait are living in hope of landing a big fish, and we sincerely trust that they will not have the mortification of finding that they have been water-bitten.

TO-DAY we furnish our readers with a Map of the Seat of War, which has been shifted from the banks of the Nile to the country lying between Suakim and Tamai, the head- quarters of OSMAN DIGMA.. There has been some very severe fighting within the past eight days—the enemy, terribly as he has been punished, re-appearing again, fear- lessly brave and reckless of death. It is estimated that 1.500 of OSMAN DIG'S troops were slaughtered in the battle which took place on Friday, and that the number of wounded was proportionately large. The British escaped on this occasion with com- paratively few casualties ; but our troops were less fortunate on Sunday, when a trans- port zareba was attacked about seven miles from Suakim. The outposting seems to have been bad, for it is stated that whilst the troops were at work one man was speared
