Indeed, the attack was altogether a surprise, and the latest reports show that, including camp-followers, some 200 men were killed on the side of the British before the rebels were driven off. There appears also to have I been a wholesale slaughter of camels, some 600 of these valuable animals having been either killed, or hamstrung so as to render them useless. It is not unlikely that this was the main object of the attack, and, if so, it must be admitted that it was successful. But the Arabs paid dearly for their tem- porary victory, for the British soon rallied, and the natives were finally repulsed with great loss. On Tuesday there was more fighting, an attack being made on a convoy which resulted in some 400 Arabs being slain during the wil hering fire to which they were subjected, On Wednesday Hasheen, which' was occupied as the result of the victory on Friday, was evacuated in consequence of the difficulty of keeping up communication.' People are beginning to ask—What is to be the outcome of all this slaughter? If the railway to Berber is to be thus laid in fire and blood, it will become memorable as the most costly line of communication which the world has known.

I A LAZY CASUAL —Thomas Turner. a tramp, was brought ' before Mr. G. L. Davies at Runcarn Police Court OR Thurs- day, and was sentenced to seven days' hard lebeur for re- fusing to perform his task at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning, after sleeping in the casual ward all night. THE NUISANCE INSPECTORSHIP AT RUNCORN.—At a meeting on Thursday morning the Highway and Sanitary , Committee of the Improvement Commissioners r which can- sists of the whole Board) decided to recommend Mr James Percival, of Church-street, for the appointment of nuisance inspector. There were nearly 50 applications. WESTON TOWNSHIP MEETING.—The annual vestry meet- ing for Weston was held on Thursday evening in the Netional Schoolroom. The Rev J J Bryant presided, and there was a good attendance. It was resolved to submit to the magistrates the following names for the selection of overseers :—Messrs Edward Aaron, Thomas Ford (retiring overseers), J W Kirkham, William Armstrong, James Ford, and L Rosenberg. Mr E Aaron was appoiated as- sessor of taxes, and Mr James Collier collector of assessed taxes. Captain Clarke was appointed waywarden. " UNION " TENT OF RECHAEITES, RUNCORN.—The yearly financial report of this Order has recently been published. It shows that with a balance of £243 9s 10s in hand on the let January, 1884, tee total income has been £403 Is sp. Allowances for sick and funeral expenses have amounted to £126 19s 11d, a balance of £276 Is 6id being left. The number of members stands at 131, the value of the tent being £2 4s 411 per member. The average amount paid in sick allowances during the year was 10e 61, and the aver- age for the pest nine years 6e 6J. The average age of the members of the lodge is 24 years. THE LEIGH DIVISION OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE.— The Conservatives of the Leigh division have just comple- ted the formation of a Council to work the first election in the newly-assigned district, having held meetings in all the townships and appointed representatives on the basis of five to every thousand of the population. The concluding meet- ing was held on Friday evening at Culcheth, Mr Joseph Hartley, jun , presiding. She Chairman sail they had heard their association called a caucus, but they would be an iadependent organisation following the opinions of their great leaders in Parliament, beyond that they would not be led by anyone. Mr F E Johnson and Alr Welter Cope- land, of Kenyon Hall, also addressed the meeting. SERVICE or Some .AT RUNCORN.—A good audience as- sembled in the Greenway Primitive Methodist Chapel on Wednesday to listen to a service of song entitled "Eva." The story, which has been completed and arranged from Uncle Tom's Cabin, is a very pathetic one,and was read with much ability by Mr J Humphreys, those prrsent being deeply affected. The musical portion was rendered by the choir, assisted by a few friends and the scholars, under the able conductorship of Mr T Pool, the various excerpts being given in a highly creditable manner. Mr H Giounds offi- ciated at the organ. Mr Humphreys, at the close, Wan heartily thanked for his services as reader ; and a similar compliment was paid to the conductor and choir, to which Mr T Pool responded. MISSIONARY MEETINGS AT RUNCORN.—The annual se- mons in aid of the United Methodist Free Church Home and Foreign Missions were preached in Ellesmere-street Chapel on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev W VAUSP, pastor, and in the evening by the Rev J Lewis, of Frod- sham. There were good congregations at each service, and collections were made. On Monday evening a public meet- ing was held, under the presidency of Mr G Bellamy, and addresses were delivered by the Rev G Lewis and the Rev J Naylor, of Crewe.—A missionary meeting was held in St John's Presbyterian Chapel on Monday evening. There was a good attendance' and Mr James Pritchard occupied the chair. The Rev J Roberts, formerly a missionary in Khassia, India, delivered an interesting address upon his labours, and at the close was heartily thaaked. The col- Wan on behalf et Presbyterian Mission work realised 13 12s. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Thursday under the presidency of Mr Bradabaw. Present : Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs J Brock, H W Deacon, J B Imison, Glover, Davies, Shaw, and Denby (clerk )—The District Education Committee reported that during February there were 102 applications for school fees, which were re- commended to be paid in 92 cases. Fifty-one persons were convicted for contravention of the Education Act.—The re- port was adopted, on the motion of Mr H W Deacon.—The Salary of attendance officer, Mr Henry Davies, was increased according to the scale of the Board, having completed his Bth year —On the recommendation of the School Manage- ment Committee William Thomas was appointed a month on trial as caretaker of the West Bank Schools at a salary of El 53.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £5OO 03 3d. During the past month there had been £ll9 received from school fees It was also recommended that the Board be empowered to ob- tain a loan of £1,400 from the Public Works Loan Com- missioners for the additional accommodation required at the West Bank School and the necessary furniture and fittings, repayable by equal instalments of principal in 30 years with Interest at 31 per cent.—The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Dr O'Keeffa.—Mr Glover remarked that there had not yet been a report presented with regard to the school of Cookery, and he wished to know whether there had been anything received for the sale of the pies and various dishes cooked.—The Clerk replied that the way in which the school was worked was this. He gave the mis- tress £3 for each school,•and she bought the articles for cooking, and then sold them to the children. During the last six months the Cooking School had made a profit of 2J; the six months previously there was a loss of 2d ; so that up to the present time there was a loss of a half•penny. (Laughter.) The Chairman would give a report upon the school at the end of the year.—This concluded the business. RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN. The annual vestry meeting for the township of Runcorn, was held io Bethesda schoolroom on Thursday evening. Mr W Hand- ley occupied the chair. Messrs C Cooke, and J J Speak. men, were appointed to audit theaccounts of the Burialßoard, and it was decided that they should present their report at a meeting to he held on the 16th Apd..—The Chairman in a brief spsech referred to the excellent manner in which Mr W Sutton, the assistant overseer, performed his duties, and said the auditor at the last audit expressed a wish that the books of every township were kept in the same neat , and accurate way. (Applause.) During the year ended on Wednesday the receipts had been as follows :—Oa March' 26th. 1884, there was a balance at the bank to the credit of the township of £530 18s 7d. and daring the year the poor II rates had produced £3850 7s Bd, making a total capital of £4 385 18s. There had been paid to the Board of Guar- dians £3,049, to the Runcorn Burial Board £l2O, to the Runcorn School Board £350, for removal of offices to the Town Hall, and purchase of necessary furniture £36 2s 11d, and for rent, registration expenses, salary of assistant over- seer £268 3s 7d. There was a balapce at the bank to the credit of the township of £5132 Is 3d. In answer to a ques- tion the chairman said the amount of irrecoverable rates, a large ptoportioa of which was for empty and insanitary property, was £l6O. Property not intended to be occupied again had to remain on the valuation list, and the effect of this was that owners of occupied houses had to pay the rates of unoccupied houses. The justices had excused rates amounting to £6 6s.—This was con- sidered highly satisfactory. —lt was then decided to submit to the magistrates the followinEe names of persons eligible to serve as overseers : Messrs W Handley, W Whittaker (retiring overseers), Thos Boote, E Imison, 8 Taylor, and William Fisher. Speeches highly eulogising the ability and services of Mr Whittaker and Mr Handley were made by Mr (.1 Moss and Mt E Imi- eon. The latter gentleman wished it to be distinctly under- stood that his name was not placed upon the list in opposition to the retiring overseers.—The Chairman ob- served that Mr Whittaker and himself could not but feel highly gratified at the eulogies passed upon them.—Mr John Simpson was reappointed assessor of taxes, and Mr W Sutton (assistant overseer) collector of assessed taxes.— Mr Moss, in proposing Mr Sulon, said the sooner the taxes and the collector of assessed taxes were abolished and the better.—Several ratepayers concurred.—A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. MAsostlo FUNERAL AT RUNCORN.—The mortal remains of Mr Robert Rigbv, of the London and North-Western Hotel, Runcorn, were interred at the Runcorn Cemetery on Thursday afternoon in the presence of a large assemblage of people. After but a few weeks' suffering from brain fever and congestion of the lungs, Mr Rigby died on Monday morning at the comparatively early age of 39. He was highly esteemed in the town, was a prominent member of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons, Runcorn, and his early demise is lamented by a large circle of friends. A number of years ago, the Freemasons, as a body, ceased to exist in the town, but through the influence and the earnest and ' persistent efforts of the deceased gentleman, the Ellesmere Lodge was resuscitated, and is now in a most flourishing condition. Daring „his lifetime Mr Rigby was W.M. to the Ellesmere Lodge. and was P.P.G D. of Cheshire. When the funeral cortege departed from the late residence of the de- ceased, rain was descending in a steady downpour, but the route to the Camstery was nevertheless lined by hundreds lof spectators, and a large crowd had also gathered in the vicinity of the grave. The procession was headed by the Rev R Edwards and Dr Carruthers (the deceased's medical attendant), and about 20 members of the Valley Lodge of Oddfellows, G.U. Order. Next in order were the following .Masonic hrethren :—The Rev J Lockwood, P. 13 .0 , R Old- bury, W.M.; E Marwood, ; J W Coxhill, P.M.D.O ; W Mellor, P.M. ; Richard Clarke, sour, P.M.; G Moss, P.M.; W R Wass, P.M.; G Bell, J.W.; G Summerfield, S.D.; F A Lake, J.D. ; T H Annett, J.B. ; J K Digges, P.M P.P.A.D C. ; W Houghton, Tyler, W Timmins, R Clarke, janr, James Littler, It Gore, J D Davies, J Collier,J J Waterworth, R Evans, J Le Coutier, W W Copland, W.M. (1,384), A. Woolrich, (1,3861, T 11 Hitchen (secretary Cholmondeley Lodge), W Harrington (418), and W Garnett. Each member wore the mourning emblem of the order and a sprig of acasia. Following were a number of tradesmen and licensed victuallers, amongst them being Messrs W Coward, P Wright, T Lydiate, W Anderton, W Green, J 0 Unsworth, W G Cunningham, and W Hankinson. Walking behind the hearse were Captain 11 Rigby, Messrs C Rigby, W H Roberts, James Rigby, T Price, D Price, John Price, Davies, John Leicester, W Pritchard, M Barker, W Sutton, J J Speakman, Sykes, and Andrews. The body was enclosed in a shell, a leaden coffin, and an outer coffin of oak mounted in brass, the whole being supplied by Mr W Brown, of Bridgewater-street. The bearers were eight intimate friends of the deceased. Mr J Knowles, formerly of Runcorn, had charge of the arrangements. The service at the grave side was conducted by the Rev R Edwards, assisted by the Rev J Lockwood. The feneral service of the Oddfellows was ' read by Brother William Littler. The Rev R Edwards also delivered an impressive funeral oration. BAY'S COMPOUND, a demulcent anodyne, expectorant, for Cough and Colds. Sold by all Chemists, 90, ls, IsAd, Is 9d. --Advt.
HAGUE'S MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN —This well-known troupe of minstrels gave a capital performance at the Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday evening. There was a

large audience. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Mr G. El Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the folio wing persons for neglect- ing to send their children regularly to school :—John Bar- rett, William donee, Hugh Nixon' Samuel Hunt, Henry Davies, William Caine,Wra. Bailey Christopher Buchanan, Samuel Burrows Hugh Gallagher, Dunne, and John Daley (two case;), The cases were proved by attendance officers Messrs. Davies, Joynson, and Rowe, and the usual fine et 5s was imposed. CAMDEN SUNDAY SCHOOL BRAES BAND.—With the ob- ject of raising funds towards obtaining this band new and and additional instruments, a concert was given in Bethesda schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. T. Norman occupied the chair, and there was a moderate attendance. Under the leadership of Mr J Ainsworth, the band rendered several selections in creditable style. Songs, lec, were given by the following :—Messrs It Morris, R Moore, C Pownall, A E Hawkins, A Fox, C Nickson, Mrs R Moore, Mr e T Burrows, and Mies Curzon. Mr John Ravenscrott ac- companied. ASSAULTING A Srterga AT Rtsconw.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on lifoeclay, James Caffey, a young man, was charged with assaulting his sister, Ellen Ciffey.—The de- fendant pleaded guilty.—Oa Saturday morning the parties were at thelr mother's house in Back Mersev-etreet, when the defendant made certain allegations against his sister, which she denied. He thereupon struck her several times on the face, cutting her lip.—The Chairman (Mr Henry Reynolds) characterised the assault as a brutal one, and fined the defendant 40s and costs, or in default a month's hard labour.—He went to gaol. THEATRES AND THIEVING: A WIDNES CASE.—At Whines Police Court on Thursday, before Messrs F H Gossage and H Gaskell, junr, JAM!' Grant, 15 years of age, was charged with stealing 14lbe of scrap iron from the West Bank Dock, the property of Major James Cross and others. On the 24th lost, Richard Hughes, an employe at the docks, saw the prisoner picking up the iron. Subsequently P.C. Holbrook apprehended the prisoner, who, in answer to the charge, siid he hid stolen the iron in order to get money to go to the theatre. He intended, he said, to take the iron to Carley's marine store.—He was sentenced to seven darn' hard la- bour.

A DANGEROt7S SLEEPING PLACE AT WIDNES. For a long period the Widnes Bench of magistrates have endeav- oured to stamp out the dangerous practice of sle•.ping in chemical works, with only partial success, bet an incidest occurred at the works of Messrs Mnsp-att on Smiley, which Wit no doubt have a deterrent eff-xt. Late on Saturday night a tramp named Fraecis Murray arrived in the town and went to a common lodging-house, but in coneequence of his behaviour, he was eurneel out. He then went to Messrs Mutpratts' works, :and about throe o'c'ock he wee awakened from sleep and told a policemen was in search of him. He ran away, and in his hurry fell into a tank of boiling water. He was terribly scalded up to the waist, and Dr. Cooper having dressed his wounds, Mr. Scannell bad him removed to the Workhouse hospital. INSANITARY PROPERTY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, R chard Mclntyre, of Rochdale, was summoned by the W.dnes Local Board with committing a breach of the Public Health Act.—Mr J T Allen, clerk to the Local Board, prosecuted, and the defendant was en- represented—Mr Allen stated that the defendant owned two oettages in Grenfell.straet, which were in a very insanitary condition. The matter lead been before the Beard for the past three months, and a for:night ago the defendant's solicitors promised that the necessary work should be dorm forth w ith, and to pay the costs of the police proceedings. This agreement. howeve-, had not be-n evried out. Mr. Allen pointed out that the dereTiaot was liable to a penalty of IS, but Lb. Bud al not As% to press for ths full pen .Itv —they wished the pelal;c to un lerst.nd teat breaches of the Public Health Ac would no- 10 tolerated—Evidence having been given by Mr D.ckson, the sanitary inspector, and Dr Cooper, midical officer ef health, the Bench made an order for the abatement of the nuisance, and ordered the defendant to pay costs. • WESLEYAN SUNDAY Smarm, RIINCORN.—The annual meeting of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit Sunday School Union was held in Brunswick Schoolroom on Thursday evening. Tea was provided by Mr Robert Shaw, and a large number of teachers availed themselves of his hospital- ity. Subsequently the Rev E J Robinson occupied the chair and delivered an address. Mr R Shaw spoke upon the 'present state of Sunday schools. The report of the school inspectors (Mr P. Shaw and Mr Hedley Fitton) was read by Mr Fitton. It showed that the Sunday schools comprised in the Union had an aggregate of 235 teachers and 2,287 scholars, and an average attendance, morning and afternoon together, at each school, of 139. The report offered several suggestions on the proper method to be pur- sued in the religions instruction of children, especial stress being laid upon the importence of jadicious questioning. In regard to the good order of the schools visited, the inspectors gave the palm to the country schools. In conclusion, the inspectors stated that as a whole the Sunday schools were ia a most healthy and praiseworthy state. Several , addresses were delivered, and the inspectors were thanked for their services. Mr R Shaw and Mr A Harrison were re-appointed inspectors for the ensuing year. Messrs S Pope and E Taylor were elected secretaries of the Union. The cordial thanks of those present were accorded to Mr and Mrs Shaw for providing the tea. A HEARTLESS MOTHER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Monday, before Mr. H. Gaekell, jour., and Mr. J. Brock, Elizabeth Peacock, 42 years of age, a widow, lately living at Terrace-row, Widnes, was charged with deserting her four children.—Mr. J. Scannell, relieving officer, said on the 19th December, 1883, his attention was called to the prisoner's children, whom he found in an empty house in Terrace-row. They were in a shocking state—hungry, dirty, and nearly naked. The eldest child said his mother had been away about a week, and he and the other children were supported by people bringing broken bread. All his (witness's) efforts to find the prisoner were unavailing un- til be recently discovered she was living in Runcorn. About fifteen months ago she was left a widow, and shortly after- wards she applied to the Guardians for outdoor relief, but it was discovered that she had been imprisoned several times, on the last occasion for eight months for robbery from the person, and the Guardians, under the circumstances, thought she was not a fit person to receive outdoor relief. They therefore told her to become an inmate of the house, but she refused, and shortly afterwards deserted her family. Widows of an honest, industrious character were readily granted outdoor relief by the Guardians, who to further encourage them also paid the school fees of their children. —The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. FRODSHAM TOWNSHIP MEETING.—The annual meeting of ratepayers was held at the Town Hill on Wednesday, Mr Thomas Davies in the chair. Mr John Ashton and Mr Thomas Hadfield were nominated as guardians for the en- suing year, and Mr James Andrews and Mr r Davies as overseers. Mr Andrews, it was stated, had held the office for about half a century.-04 the motion cf Mr C E Lena- her, seconded by Mr T Riley, the overseers were directed to ask the Sanitary Authority what amount, it any, had been apportioned to Frcdsham Lordship for right to connect the Overton sewer with Frodsham main sewer.— Mr C E Linaker, referring to the water scheme, said he understood the trial wells at Newton yielded sufficient water for the tows of Frodsham, and he suggested that it should be recommended to the Sanitary Authority to supply Frod- sham only with water. As the lordahip declined to shire any portion of the expense he did not see why the township should adopt an expensive pumping scheme when a suffi- cient supply for Frodshem could he obtained by gravita- tion.—Mr C R Linaker's suggestion was adopted.—Mr Henry Lrhaker was re-appoin•ed waywaralen. He urged that a Local Board should ha formed, as the charge for highway purposes during the past year had been £341 with only three miles of road—The follow- ing were nominated to serve oc the Local Paro- chial Sanitary Committee :—Messrs Robert Holland, Thomas Davies, and Edmund Ashworth. It was reported at a subsequent meeting that the cost -of lighting the dis.rict during the past year had been £53 19s 4d, and it was resolved that £7O should be raised for the ensuing twelve months. Dr Weaver and Mr J W Rethwell were re- appointed inspectors. PROPOSED CEMETERY FOR HALTON.—it the annutl vestry meeting for the township of Halton, held at the Nor- ton Arms on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of the Rev J Lockwood, a report was presented by the committee appointed iu 1881 to consider the advisability of forming a cemetery and Burial Board. The report stated the commit- tee had inspected two sites, but they did not meet the ap- proval of Sir Richard Brooke, who was, however, in favorer of a cemetery being provided if practicable. The com- mittee had ascertained that the surrounding and usual places of interment are gradually being closed against out- tiders,and consequently there will shortly be no near place of interment open t 3 receive their dead, with the only exe.p- tion of Runcorn Cemetery, which in all probability mIY before long, owing to its being so rapidly filled, also be closed against us as non.parishioners, even upon payment of double fees. The secretary had addressed a letter to the overseers of each township, asking whether the ratepayers would be willing to join in the formation of a cemetery,

and he had received only one answer, viz., from Stockham, the overseer of which said, " We shall be willing to join, providing the expenditure is not too heavy, as most are agreed as to the necessity of such a cemetery." Of course in the case of th 3 other townships not joining, double fees would be charged as at If—ll:learn. To provide a cemetery for the whole ecclesiastical parish it is calculated that a sum not exceeding £lOO would be required. To pay this sum off in 20 years with interest would require a rate :—lf for . . _

Halton alone, of lid. in the ; for Halton and Stockham, Id. in the £; for Halton, Stockham, and Norton, id, in the S ; and for Halton, Stockily% Norton, and Ci if too, less than Id. This amount would be lessened by sums received for zround fees from parishioners and double ground fees from outsiders. lhe importance of providing a cemetery had always been of the highest importance, and never had the necessity been more forcibly pressed upon their atten tion than at the present time, when such a sadden, serious, and extensive outbreak of measles had overtaken the parish, so that the schools for the first time in their history have had ta be closed, nearly seventy cases at least, being under medical care. The meeting then formed a Burial Board, with the Rev J Lockwood as hon. secretary. It was decided that the Mar- quis of Cholmondeiey and Captain Hazlehurst, J.P., should be written to respecting certain suitable plots of land, and that the ratepayers of Norton, Stockham, and Clifton should be asked to join in the contemplated construction of a cemetery. THE REV CANON BARCLAY has now so fas recovered hat he can leave his room. On Wednesday he was wheeled nto the open air. WESLEYAN IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WIDNEs —The fort- nightly meeting was held in Lacey-street school. on Mon- day evening, when the Rev R Harper read a paper on" The . . . . . .

young in relation to Wesleyan Methodism." licwcoart Y.M.C.A. Hiszourcer, SOCIETY.—On Thurs- day evening Captain J. Le Coutier lectured to a large num- ber of the members of this society upon 4. Two voyages to Syria and Palestine." Mr. F. A. Lake presided.

g2The remains of Mrs. Mary Emery, who had reached the advanced age of 86, were interred in the burial ground of Bethesda Chapel on Tuesday. Since the erection of this chapel in 1835 the deceasedlady had been a member of the congregation. THE Dlaw MAGISTRATES.-The names of the following gentle- men were yesterday morning formally inserted in the corn.. mission of the peace for the borough of Warrington : Conn. John Greening, Bewsey-road ; Conn. John Platt, Mount Walton ; Mr. Edwin James Guest, 8.A., Egypt- Street; Major John Richard Pickmere, Latchford. THE APPOINTMENT OF A RELIEVING OFFICER FOR RUN- CORN.—For the vacant position of relieving officer for Ran- corn no leas than 97 applications had been received up to yesterday afternoon. To-day theecommittee appointtd by the Board of Guardians will consider the applications, and report to the Board GU Tuesday next. One applicant is a major in the Artillery. Tun BASIS OF COUNTY RATE.—Yesterday Mr W Hand- ley and Mr Henry Linaker appeared before the County Justices at Chester Sessions, on behalf of the Runcorn Union, to appeal against the new basis of county rating, on the ground that the assessments were too high. The argu- ments of the deputation were so eff c ive that the magis- trates adjourned consideration of the subject, and in the meantime the figures will be thoroughly gone into. THE FORTHCOMING HOLIDASS.—The London and North- Western Railway Company advertise a cheap excursion for Thursday next to London and a number ef other plac..s of interest, and another excursion for Birmiagham and other places on Good Friday. By the Cheshire Lines on Good Friday, and the following Satarday and Monday, cheap ex- altation tickets will be issued from Warrington to Liverpool and Southport. Further particulars will be found in our advertising columns. THE BLOCKING OF WEST BANK STREET, WIDNES —4 meeting between representatives of the Local Board, Messrs Bolton and Son, and the various eersons interes.ed in the West Bank•street property, took place at Alforde Cham- bers on Thursday afternoon. There was consideraule dis- cussion upon the difficulty that has arisen, bat those pre- sent failed to arrive at any decision, and the Highway Committee will further consider the matter, and make a recommendation to the Board.

TOwNSIIIP MEETING AT iTALTON.—The annual town- ship m,•eting was held on Tuesday evening at the Norton Arms Hotel. The following persons were nominated as overseers :—Messrs. T. Wright, Hugh Rowe, Wm. Nicksen, John Rutter, John Bagulev, and J4seph Astbury. Mr. W. W. Haddock was re-appointed waywarden. Messrs. T. Wright and Woo. Nickson were appointed assessors of land and taxes; Messrs. George Riley and Tnomas Potter, Con- stables; and Messrs. John Ratter and Juha Ragaley, bur- levrnen. _ _

TEE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.---The nominatione for this annual contest have now closed. The gentlemen selected by the Rival Retepayers' Association, whose names have already beeen published in The Examiner, are the only nersons nominated. Elo far the contest promises to be of a very quiet description. The Hope of Appleton Lodge of Good Tempters have passed a resolution to oppose the return of Mr W .1 Hargreaves, who is a publican, both by recording tivir individual vot*s against him and other means. THE ELECTION OF RUNCORN GUARDIANS.—Yesterday was the last day for the nominat4cn of pers.•r s to serve as Guardians for the Runcorn Union. We undeistand there will be contests at Frodsham and Frodsharn Lordship, and very probably at Runcorn, as it is stated there are six gen- tlemen nominated for the five seats. Amongst these are four retirieg Guardians, Viz, Messrs W Handley, W Fisher, W Whittaker, and T Norman; and T Boots and S Taylor. At Weston there will be no contest, the Rev J J Bryant and Mr E Aaron being nominated. The Rev Canon Barclay does not seek re-election. Tim Homa 'sox TRAM—The English iron market is dull, and, owing to the rumours of war, very uneettled, and the fear is openly expressed that an outbreak of hostilities would make matters worse than they are, which is saying a great deal. The pt-iron market has been inanimate. The Glasgow warrant market, after being dull, with a declining tendency, for a time became strong, owing to a rumour, which turned out to be merely a rumour, that a large pig. iron company were likely to blow out their furnaces. Otherwise there is no new feature in the Scotch trade, busi- ness being as bad as it can well be. Closing buyers of war- rants on Wednesday were 41s ld cash, and 41s 91 a month; sellers a'sking one half-penny per ton more. The North of England pig-iron market is still very lifeless, but prices are unchanged —lron. ALLEGED HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT WIDNES.—OR Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Patrick McCabe, 19 years of age, of Timperley-street, formerly a soldier, was charged with stealing a silk pocket handkerchief and a purse containing Is Gd from the person of Michael Murphy, labourer, War- rington-road, Widnes. The prisoner was also charged with I assaulting Murphy.—From a statement made by Inspector Wood it appeared that about half-past seven on the night of Sunday, the 15th lost, Mu phy was on his way home near the Adelphi Hotel, when the prisoner came up to him and said "Will you give me the price of a drink ?" Murphy replied that he could not, whereupon the prisoner struck him a severe blow on the head with his fist, knock- ing him to the ground. While in this position the prisoner also struck him on the left eye. He felt the prisoner's hands in his left coat pocket in which was the handkerchief and purse containing is 6d, and he saw the prisoner walk away wine them in his hand. He subsequently gave information to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Pitt. Whilst on the way to the police station the prisoner said "I wonder if he has got any witnesses, for I am well sure he only saw me himself.—This statement was borne out by the evidence of Murphy, and corroborative testimony was given by John Finlan, Murphy-street, Jane Finlan, Caroline Bannon, and Hannah Needham, wife of Matthew Needham, of Grove-street; and P.C. Pitt.—Mr J W Knowles represented the prisoner, and in defence said the two men had a quarrel some short time ago, and this case was a trumped up story by the prosecutor in order to have his revenge —The magistrates committed the prisoner to the avizes for trial, but admitted him to bail in two sureties of £5O each.

IF You WANT GOOD CASKS of any description, or tabs, er timber, apply to Mr. Joseph Anderson's Cooperage, Apple- ton-street, Widnes. Cheapest terms in the town.—Advt. "THE BUSINESS OF THE OHURCII."—We take the follow- ing from Truth :—" Speaking on Wesleyan Methodism at St Helens, the other day, the Bishop of Liverpool said that he hoped that every man would feel that he was a partner in the business of the Church. Now, of course, there are partners and partners, but a man who draws nothing at all out of a business can hardly be expected to work with the same amount of energy and earnestness as the man who draws his thousands annually. The Bishop will de well to Ignlember this little fact." RuNCOale Rolle) Or COMMISSIONERS —A special meeting of the Board of Improvement Commissioners was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Monday morning. Mr R Shaw presided, and there were present Messrs Pritchard, Speakman, Lake, White, Dobeon, Norman, Williams, Linaker (law clerk), and Brookes (secretary). The meeting was called for the purpose of piecing various accounts to close the financial year. The Secretary reported that the Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounta amounting to £217 is 11d, and that the list of irrecoverable rates, amouniing to .£lB4 Pa 00, he allowed.—The Chairman said these accounts included the payment of £4O to Mr Stethem on hospital account, and an item of £45 3e, the ex- pense of taking the poll in connection with the Ship Canal Lake said this amount was less than was ex- pected —The Secretary said the extra cost respecting the Ship Canal in consequence of the poll amounted to between £52 and £s3.—Mr Norman moved, and Mr Lake secended, that the accounts be passed, and the motion was carried.— A resolution of thanks to the Board of Guardians for kindly allowing the use of their election bags in the taking of the poll was passed on the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr Dobson. SERVICE OF SONG AT WIDNES.—With the object of rais- ing funds towards the clearing off of the debt upon the Pri- mitive Methodist Chapel, Hutchinson-street, Widnes. a ser- vice of song entitled "Eva, or Uncle Tom's Cabin," was given in that place of worship on Tuesday evening. There was a fair attendance, and Mr B Dutton presided. In open- jog the proceedings the chairman delivered a short address in which he stated that there was a population of 23,000 people in Widnes. There were only 17 churches and chapels in the town affording accommodation for 8,700 wor- shippers. People sometimes asked where the remainder of the population went to on a Sunday, and the reply was that they were at work. This he considered a sad state of things, and he expressed his conviction that if a deputation waited upon the employers they would give their men one day's rest out of the seven. He urged the Primitive Methodist to continue labouring with the sem@ zealous spirit to aid movements of a progressive character, and he had no doubt the result would be larger congregations and more churches and chapels.—The touching Mary of Eva was then read by the Rev J Hothersalh the musical portion of the service being rendered by the choir, assisted by friends from other churches. The string band in connection with the chapel did good service. The usual votes of thanks were ac- corded. VOLUNTEER FUNERAL AT HALE—On Sunday afternoon the remains of Ellis Hughes, whose death took place dur- ing last week, were interred at Hale church with military honours. The deceased was a member of No. 2 battery of the 6th Lancashire Artillery Volunteers, and the proceed- ings attracted a large concourse of spectators, to the number of nearly a thousand. About 100 members of the company from Gersten, Widnes, and the neighbourhood of the vil- lage met at the Drill shed, and marched from there to the residence of the deceased. The procession then left the house in the fcllowing order :—The firing party, with arms reversed, to the number of 14; the drum and fife band of the corps from Gersten, playing the "Dead March " ; the body, borne by eight members of the corps, on the coffin be. lug placed the Union Jack as a pail, and the helmet and accoutrements of the deceased; closely followlog the body were the deceased's relatives and friends. The rest of the corps brought up the rear of the procession. Arriving at the church, the service for the dead was gone through by the Rev. R. B. Stewart. When the body was lowered into the grave three volleys were fired by the firing party as a last tribute to the memory of the deceased. The corps was , commanded by Captain Williams, Sergeant-Major Price (of Hale), Sergeant-Major Tamer, and Sergeant-Major Harri- son (of Garston). THE NEW PUBLIC OFFICES FOR WIDNES —A Special meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held on Thursday, Mr F II Gossage in the chair. Present—Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs Carey, Handley, Sadler, Wright, Midwood, Ciaskell, junr, Martley. Webster, and T Allen (clerk). A letter was read from Mr S B Previa, of the Local Government Board, who said the Board understand that the offices pro- posed to be provided were intended not only for the use of the Local Board, but also for the Widnes School Board. The Board was advised that it was doubtful whether the local Acts authorise the construction of offices other than those required for the use of the Local Board, and the Board have therefore inserted provisional article I. of the draft, which wilt remove any doubt as to the power of the Local Board to provide offices for any public purposes. As however, no reference to such an extension of the powers Of the local Acts was made, either in the application of the Local Board, or in the advertised notice of the inquiry, it would be neces- sary, in the event of the Local Board desiring article I. of the draft to be retained, that a further notice of the pro- posed alteration in the local Acts should be advertised. The General Purposes Committee had considered this question, and on the motion of Mr Carey, seconded by Mr Handley, it was decided that application should be made to the Local Government Board to provide that in any provisional order about to be issued, that section 28 of the Widnes Improve- ment Act, HU, be so altered to enable the Local Board to provide offices for any other public purpose. A:letter was also read from the Local Government Board with reference to the loan for the erection of the public offices, and on the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee it was resolved that application should be made for an inquiry to ' be held upon the question. Tile Runooner GAS BlLL.—This bill come on Monday before Sir Arthur Otway, the chairman of committee in the House of Commons, as an unopposed measure. Mr Curry attended as parliamentary agent for the Bill, and Mr G W Stevenson as consulting engrneer to toe promoters. The bill seeks power to increase the capital of the company, which is at present fixed at £4OOOO, the object in view be- ing the erection of new works, to take the place of those now existing. It is estimated that two years will be oc- cupied in completing the scheme, the old works being gradually allowed to exhaust themselves. A large gas- holder will be btsilt in the first instance.—ln reply to Sir Aethur Otway, Mr Stevenson said the highest dividend the company had ever paid was 10 per cent.—Sir A Otway : What is the present price of coal at Runcorn 7—Mr Steven- son : 12a 60 per ton.—ls that at the pit mouth ?—No; the works.—What is the population of Runcorn P—Mr Curry : About 16,000,—1s that the whole of the district you supply?—Mr Stevenson: Yee. The population at the last census was 14,000; the whole population in the limits of supply will be from 17,000 to 18,000.—Sir A Otway sug- gested thaa the statutory minimum power of the gas sup- plied should be 16 candle-light, instead of 14 candle-light as proposed in the bill. The promoters had offered to make the minimum 13 candle-light ; but as they are now sugply- ing gas equal to 18 candle-light, the Chairman thought 16 candle-light a reasonable minimum. No other point was raised ; and the bill was approved without alteration' the Chairman remarking that it was a very fair bill. 'I here were present a deputation, consisting of Messrs F Rigby, J.P., James Handley, J.P., R B Toft, and J 11 Frith, of Runcorn ; Mr Stevenson, gas engineer, of Parliament-street, London, and Mr Robert Davies' solicitor, Warrington. The bill was reported to the House the same evening.

Bright, William Hem y Bann Coulter, station master at Appleton, on the London and North- department, Lime-street Station, prosecuted, narrated the circumstances of the case, and said he could prove six separate offences ag eWeabaietnzeszrtillitni the prisoner, who appeared to have reduced his ap- propriations of moniy to a system.—Alexander Gunning, detective officer on the London and North-Western Rail- way, stationed at Wigan, said on the 18th February he took llic.elCateeVa'' snton, sums jurt o rf., n a ticket from Wigan to St. Helens, and went forward to Appleton by the 5-47 pen. train. On arriving there the prisoner charged him 61 excess fare, which he paid. The prisoner did not give him a receipt for the money.—John Hoare, chief clerk in the ticket audit department, Ruston. produced the excess fare-book sent from Appleton. The 61. paid by the last witness was not entered.—The prisoner was then fermally charged. He elected to ha dealt with by the magistrates, and pleaded guilty.—Gher offences of a similar nature were then gone luta—William Hale, detective officer, Warrington, said on the 24th February he booked from Southport to St. Helens, and travelled on to Appleton.. He paid the prisoner 61. excess fare.—Arthur Harvey, night watchman, Park-lane Station, Liverpool, deposed that on the 26:h February he travelled frolt nkelmersiale to Apple- ton, where he gave up a ticket to St. Helens. He paid the prisoner 61. excess fare.--JosePh James, gateman, Lime. street Station. on the sth March travelled from St. Helens to Appleton by the 8-5 p.m. train. lie prodeced a ticket issued between Skelmeesdale and St. Helens, and paid the prisoner 61. excess fare.—Themas Woed, detective. , sergeant, Lime-street, on the same day travelled from St Helens to Appleton with a ticket issued to Sutton Oak, and paid de Hill on xon"t" fare.—Jackson Jeffreys night watchman, E he 13th March travelled to Appleton with a tic- ket from St. Helens to Clock Face, and paid to the prisoner prisoner said he was exceedingly sorry for vi 3j excess fare.—John Hoare proved that these amounts were nor accounted for in the prisoner's excess book.— Detective Inspector Richards deposed to apprehending the service with the company and the good character he had borne. He pleaded on behalf of his wife and children, who were strangers in the locality, that the Bench would only inflict a fine, so that he would have a chance to retrieve his name and character. It was the first time he bad been before a bench of magistrate.: in his life.—Mr Preston pointed out that the prisoner, as station master, had complete charge of the arrangements at Apple- ton, and under these circumstances he pressed the charge.— The prisoner made a statement to the elect Veat ever since he hid been at Appleton be had had dishoneit people work- inghe song with him.—Detective-inspector Richards re called said the prisoner had borne a good character.—Mr Preston : He has been in the service of the company fo: 14 years.—Mr Brock said the offence was a very serious one, especially considering the position the prisoner had occupied, and the fact of his long service rather aggravated the offence. Tha Bench did not think it was a case for a fine, but they would not inflict the full penalty of three months' had labour in consideration of his long service nnder the company.—The, prisoner was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne Flenlkes. APPLICATION rose A NEW TRIAL.—MI Wharton, barris- ter, Manchester (instructed by Messrs Anderton and Don. nolley, Bury), applied for a new trial in an action brought by Messrs Cliffs ant Son, clay pipe manufacturers, Leeds and Halton, near Runcorn, against Messrs Hutchinson and Meson, chemical manufacturers, Tottington, near Bury, to recover the earn of £32 ls 4d, for two clay worms. At the last court day the defendants did not appear, nor were they represented, and Mr W H Lin titer, solicitor, who appeared for the plaintiffs, secured a verdict for £26 Os Id, the sum of £6 le3 having been paid into court. Mr Wharton now explained to his honour that he and his clients did not arrive at the court before the donclusion of the business, in consequence of missing a train at Manchester, and in support of his application for a new trial, contended that Messrs Hutchinson and Mason had a good defence to the action on its merits.—Mr Muliholland. barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Messrs Linaker and Linaker, Runcorn), urged that if his honour was disposed to grant a new trial it would be upon payment of plaintiff's costs for the first hearing and the present application.—His honour said this was a case in which as a rule be should not grant a new trial, and he did not wish to make this a precedent. Still, as teere seemed to be merits to fight about, whether successfully on the part Of the defendant or not he could give no opinion now, he had no objection to granting the application, under the circum- stances, because the non-attendance of the defendants at the last hearing seemed to have arisen through an accident on the part of the counsel. The new trial, be added, must be on the terms of payment of the costs of the former trial and the present application. ACTION A6AINST A FRODSHAM MERCHANT. John Priestmer. farmer and butcher, Frodsham, sued John S Rim- met, corn and seed merchant, Frodshatn, for £2 4s, the bal- ance of an account for corn and oats supplied. Mr. Hitchen appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Burton represented the defendant. From Mr. Hitchen's statement it appeared that during the first week in September the defendant agreed to purchase all the stock of the plaintiff's .wheat and oats, the oats at 2s 10d and the wheat at 4s 11d. Afterwards the de-

fendant said the wheat and corn was better than the sample and was of beautiful quality. The corn was delivered in various quanaties to the defendant's crier, and in the month of October the defendant paid £l5O en account. In Novem- ber the plaintiff asked for the balance, £2B 7s, and the de- fendant demurred and attempted to raise up the question of the quality of the corn. Ha sent the plaintiff what he cal- led a corrected invoice, and wished a halfpenny per bushel to be taken off the oats and the wheat: The plaintiff never consented to such an arrangement, and the defendant paid a cheque for £26 Sc, leaving the balance now sued for.—The plaintiff corroborated this statement. He was cross-exam- ined by Mr. Burton to show that the cereals were not opal to sample, but the witness maintained that both the oats and wheat were better than sample. After hearing the evi- , dance for the defence, his Honour said if the plaintiff thought the cheque did not settle the balance due it was his diev to return it, but having kept the cheque and cashed it, he accepted the conditions under which it was paid, and he could not now sue for anything more. A verdict for the defendant was entered. INTERESTING ACTIONS.—A WIFE'S DEALINGS —Messrs Peter Smith and Ca, chemists and druggists, High-street, Runcorn, sued Mr Henry Watkin, commission agent, Hal- ton, for the sum of £3 7s id, for goods supplied.—Mr Bur- ton appeired for the plaintiffs, and Mr Hitchin for the defendant. At the outset Mr Hitchin informed the court that the question at issue was whether the wife had authe.- rity to pledaa her husband's credit.—Mr Smith gave evi- dence to the effect that the defendant and his family had dealt at the shop for a considerable number of years. and up to the present account, which commenced in May, 1882, and closed in regularly.Spte m bTe eof i items paint for the garden rails, brushes, and various things of household consumption, and on one occasion the defendant s sameinci usdecadr? pto be da wecrcs o ti n for ts children,ha bnee had purchased an ounce of tobacco and a box of Beecham's pills. The wife had also borrowed 10i on the 7th Septem- ber, 1882, saying she and her husband were going by train to a distant town, and she had left her purse at home.—The

I defendant said the first intimation he had of this acconni was when he received the summons. He never knew Mr Smith until he saw him in the court, and had never been in his shop. He had never bought an ounce of tobacco in bis life, and had never taken a box of Beecham's pills. His wife had, during her lifetime, an income of her own, and he allowed her 103 per week for sugar, butter, and "oddments." He always purchased the flour, the beef, etc. He lived with his mother-in-law, in whose name the house was. He had six children. His Honaur said he could not say that there was any evi- dence that would lead him to the cmclusion that either by implication or inference or expressly the wife had authority to pledge her husband's credit.—Judgment was therefore entered for the defendant.—An action was also brought by Mr William Blythe, draper and clothier, High-street, against Mr Henry Watkin, to recover £8 3s 81. for shirts, hats, and suits of clothes supplied in 1883 —The plaintiff was represented by Mr Burton, and the defendant by Mr Hitchen.—The plaintiff deposed that on one occasion the defendant entered his shop and said there was something owing for the boys' clothing„ at the same tune promising to pay. He also told the plaintiff in future not to allow his wife to have anything, and he had not done so.—The de. fondant called said in 1883 he purchased suits of clothes for his boys at an auction in Liverpool. They were ready made. He had never seen the suits supplied by Mr Blythe that he was aware of. Be had a claim from Messrs [las. worth Bros. for seven suits supplied in the same year. He had not paid for them, nor had he been sued for them. He did not know whether his boys had worn them. He thought his wife had pledged them. He did not know of the accounts until his wife's death.—His Honour was inclined to think the prohibition was given under the circumstances stated by the plaintiff, and he therefore gave veld:a for the plain- tiff, the amount to be paid in a month.

FAILURE OF' J. W. CARLILE. At the Liverpool Binkruptcy Court, on Thursday, before Mr Registrar Bellringer, James Wallu...r Carlile, a timber merchant and contractor, carrying on business at Warring- ton-road, Widnes, came up for public examination. The Official receiver appeared in the case on behalf of the credi- tors, and Mr Draper for the debtor. The debtor commenced business in 1887, and failed in 1881, when he paid a com- position of Ts 6.1 in the pound. His total liabilities under that failure were £16,568, and assets £10,886. He estimated that after paying 74 6d composition he had about £6,652 left, consisiing of estimated values of building properties. He attributed his failure to the bad state of house property in Widnes; he could neither sell nor mortgage his proper- ties. The Official Receiver asked how it was, if values had deteriorated, the properties were put down in the present statement at a considerably higher fig&re than in the state- ment prepared in connection with the 1881. failure. The debtor explained that since 1881 the properties had been cor,pleted and w( rk done in connection with them, which added to their value. The values at which Ilia houses were put down in the statement were below what the properties were iatrinsically worth, but owing to the bad state of trade they were unsalea,2le. The present statement of affairs showed total liabilitica of £49.990, but the properties in respect of which the liabilities were incurred ought to realise £57,886. His business, trading as a timber mer- chant nut contractor, had been profitable. The examina- tion was adjourned to the 23rd April.
RATEPAYERS' MEETLNG AT WIDNES. INIERESTING DISCUSSION.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Widnes for the appointment of overseers was held in the overseers' office on Thursday afternoon. Mr James White was voted to the chair. Amongst those present were Dr. O'Keeffe, Muer& Elearey, A E Smith, John Matthews, 1' Swale, F H Pankhurst, R Whiteside, J Midwood, S Sad- ler, B Dutton, A. Cowley, and E Marston. On the motion of Mr T B Swale, seconded by Mr Whiteside, a vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring overseers, Messrs James White, John Matthews, and Alculn Cowley, for their past services.—The Chairman remarked that it would be the duty of the retiring overseers to levy the new rate, and they did not see that it would be possible to levy a rate less than that of last year. They gathered from Mr Hartley, clerk to the-Guardians, that the Union would require a similar amount to last year, when, including the coanty rate of £2,300, the Union was paid £3,700; and the requirements of the Widnes School Board had increased from £3,500 to £3600; so that it would scarcely be wise for the overseers to levy a lower rate than last year. The overseers had therefore decided to levy a rate of 2s. If trade would improve a little b the town, and the School Board would reduce their requirements instead of Wetness- ing them, it was quits possible that a rate of Is 9.1 in the would be ample for the year Me. He refeired to the fact that the overseers had new appointed the St Helens Branch of the Manchester and Salford Bank bankers to the over- seers in place of Parrs Bank, in consequence of the former paying interest upon deposits. Parrs Bank declined to do so. The interest during the past nine months had amounted to £32, which would be used in the interests of the rate- payers. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt Parrs Bank would now give similar terms, and it would be for the new overseers to:consider whether they would return to the local bank. He could not praise too highly their assistant overseer for the admirable way in which he p:iforrned his work. Anyone who thoroughly examined the books must admire the neat- ness and correctness with which they were kept. Trade bad been bad in the town, and many ratepayers had been scarcely in a position to meet large payments, and it is a great credit to Mr Goff that he had got every account in with the exception of one in dispute with the railway com- pany, and the other was a debt which would be recoverable from the new property owners in connection with Mr Car- lie's estate.—Mr Swale mentioned the difficulty t tere was in asc:rtaining the true fieancial position of the school, as no balance sheet was issued. The only one he had seen showed that one schoel hal supported itaelf, and the other two had only required £4OO between them.—Dr O'Keefe replied that the School Board had issued a balance sheet every year since its formation, and any person who took an interest in the financial affairs of Lhe School Board could see one and also examine the books kept by the clerk if he so desired. He pointed out that the expenses of the Board were increased owing to the new codes of the Education De- partment. Recently the staff of teachers had had to be in- in reference to the creased in consequence of the working hours of the teachers reducedtlon o f to h efi overseersveho urs Per day.—Mr Matthews bank- ing account, and said he thought it would be very wrong ta tbheeen ac upheld having make a further change now.—Mr Dutton expressed his ad- miration at the action.—Mr Midwood said he did not think Mr Carlisle's rates recoverable.—Mr Goff said if they could not recover the rates from the owner they could from the occupier.—Mr Carey: Yen could not enforce that.—The • Chairman: The owners would not like it. They could not get tenants under those conditions.—lt was then decided that the following list of names should be presented to the magis- trates, so that three overseers could be selected :—Messrs j Matthews, James White, Alcain Cowley, F H Panklinrst, Joshua Midwood, Robert Shaw, S B Stringer, and A E Smith.—Mr Carey pointed out the advantage that would accrue to the ratepayers if the rate was laid half-yearly, and he moved that the overseers take the matter into their consideration.—Mr Dutton seconded the motion, which was carried, and the meeting concluded.

FiRE NINE PERSONS KILLED.—The Langham Hotel, at Chicago, was burned down on Saturday night. A woman jumped from a fourth.storey window and was killed. Eight firemen and policemen were buried under the falling walls, and several were fatally injured. WYCLIFFE CHURCH BAZAAR. SPEECH BY MH: McMINNIES, M.P.

On Tuesday afternoull a bazaar in aid of Wycliffe day school extension fund was opened in the Wesleyan Schools, Bold-street. by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P. The expendi- ture which it was intended to wipe off by means of this bazaar has been caused, as explained by Mr. McMinnies in the speech reported below, by the necessity of providing such accommodation for an increasing number of scholars as would meet the requirements of the Education Depart- ment. The cost of these extensions amounts in all to about £BOO or £9OO, about half of wnich, however, has already been obtained, chiefly by private subscriptions. The main Object of the bazaar was therefore to clear off the balance still owing, but it was also hoped that, besides accomplish- ing this, a handsome sum would be left in hand to be de- voted to other purposes in connection with the Church. That these objects had engaged the sympathy of many will. jog workers was evidenced by the large number of stalls at the bazaar, which were filled to repletion with an endless variety of articles. The stalls were ten in number, and were presided over as follows : No. 1 kali (Day School) —Mrs. Oorney, Mrs. Clarke. Mrs. Coutts Mrs. Porrltt, Mr. Corney, Mr. °otitis. Miss Mtellner, M s; Swift, Miss Podmore, Miss Porritt, Miss Stanley, Miss Kate Ball, Miss Jmes, Miss Ada Porrltt, Miss Annie Place, Miss ansy Place, Miss Beside Rathbone. Miss J. Benson, Mr. A. Ball. _ _

No. 9 Stall (Young Men).—Miss Baker, Mr. B. Foreman, Mr. W. Hayee. Mr. B. Hall, Mr. W. Hewitt, Mr. A. Knowlem, Mr. R. Lowe, Mr. H. Newell, Mr. W. Perrin!, Mr. Stephenson, Mr. Cl, tindlow, Mr. Stout, Mr. J. Taylor, Mr. Yard:ev. No 3 atali.—Mrs. H. Roberts, Mrs. R. H. Pearson. Miss McKenzie, Mrs. Roberts, Miss Roberts, Miss N Roberts, Mrs. Sucliow. Miss R. Males, Miss M. Birtlee. No. 4 Stalls—Mrs. Barker. Miss Barker, Mr'. Legge, Miss Legge. Miss E. Legge. Mrs. Clay, Miss Garnett. No 5 Btall.—Mrs, Garland, Miss Harrison, Mrs. Poole, Miss Dignum, Mrs. Yossge, Miss H. Lignum. No. 6 Btall.—Mrs. F. A. Roberts, Miss Marsden, Miss Rymer. No. 7 Stall —Mrs Z. Armitage, Miss Armitage, Miss Lee, Miss I Litton.

No. 8 Stall (Refreshment.).— Mrs. J. L. Tunstall, Miss Hardaker, Mrs. W. Tuns? all, Miss C. Hardaker, Miss B Jones. Mils F. Jones, Miss Thomas. Tea and Supper Room —Mr. W. Roberts, Mrs. W. Roberts, Mr. Pennington, Mrs. Remick, Mrs. Pennington, Miss J. Dale, Miss E. Borrows. Miss Pennington, Miss 0. Bennett. No. 9 Stall (Bunday School). —Mrs. W. Wallington, Mrs. Edwards, Mrs. J. Knowles. Miss Sutton, Miss B. A. Knowles, Mrs. A. fj. Eathsyone, Miss It ahbone. _ . _ _
_ No. 10 Stall (Flowers, ac.) —Mrs. P,relval, Kiss Garner, Miss Blichenoagb.

As usual on these occasions considerable care and ingenuity had been exercised in the matter of decoration. Outside the schoolroom, Bold-street was spanned by a string of bright coloured bannerettes which tended to give the locality a cheerful and festive appearance. Immediately on entering the room, the flower tall, which was erected at the oppo- site end of the room was, perhaps, the most striking object. It was laden with a tastefully displayed mass of valuable flowers, the pretty, various-coloured petals of which formed a !flora than usually attractive feature of the bazaar. This stall was rendered more conspicuous by reason of its being surmounted by an elegantly designed and neatly finished screen which, we understand, was subsequently purchased by Mrs Wm Crosfield, of Liverpool, and presented to the Warrington Infirmary. The flowers were partly supplied by Messrs Dixon. of Chester, and partly contributed by per- sons living in this neighbourhood and others living at Man- chester and Altrincham. Apart from the stalls, the chief scene of the decorations was the front of the gallery which goes round three-fourths of the building, and the wall op- posite the entrance. The baldgess ef the wall was relieved by a trophy of flags and shields, and the front of the gallery was draped with scarlet cloth and hung with shields and flaws. These decorations were the work of Mr Dell, who, considering the shortness of the time at his disposal for making them, is to be complimented on his handl. work. On the various stalls there was a mul- titudinous variety of articles, one of the features of the bazaar at the opening being indeed the crowded appearance of the stalls. Notwithstanding this, however, the ladies in charge had displayed enough taste and judiciousness in the arrangement of their bright coloured and shapely wares to have satisfied that most exacting lover of the beautiful, Oscar Wilde himself, had he been there. Besides a repletion of the fancy and useful articles usually found at bazaars, there were on almost all of the stalls specimens of workmanship which were both rare and valuable. These included some chef arceuvres of fancy work, which must have kept many deft fingers diligently at work for many weeks pas', handseme mirrors, elaborate work tables and valuable plc'ures. On the day school stall a respleclent mirror was an attractive abject. This was beautifully framed with painted leather work and cardinal plush, the work of Mrs Dodge,Tarkersstreet. Mr. MCMINNum, M.P., who was received with applause, said: Ladles and gentlemen, I euppoee I need net tell you that the object ()titbit: bazaar is to clear off certain expensee that have been incurred in the enlargement of the day schools connected with Wycliffe Church. That enlarge- ment wee rendered necessary to accommodate the increasing number of scholars, and it was also necessary in order to i comply with the condition of the Education Department ,het melee, the schools were enlarged the annual grant would not be dontinaed. Now a considerable sum has been collected by private subscription, and as I suppose that nobody will say that the elementary education of the people is not a good object, the people who have got up this bazaar come before the public with hopes of considerable support. And I hope, and we all hope, that the result of this bazaar will be to clear off that debt, which will be a burden if it remains. (Hear, hear.) I need not not tell you that many very good people object to biz :ars as a means of raising money for charitable and religious objects. They do not see a virtue in making pin cushions, and they speak disrespectfully of antimacassars. I think they even go so far as to say that young ladies may be better employed than in working slip- pers for young gentlemen. (Laughter.) Very hard lan- guage is sometimes used in regard to those who support bazaars. We are compared to the money changers in the temple, and to those that sold doves. (Laughter.) I think it very bard that we sbeuld be compared to those who sold doves, for when I remember the very soft and gentle in- fluence which leads us willing captives to those who preside at these bazaars, lam rather disposed to say not that we sell doves, but that the doves sometimes sell us. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) I do not agree with the objections that are made to bazaars. I think the probability is that those objections arise from what were formerly abuses. I dare say in former days there were importunitiee that be- came exceedingly objectionable, but I hope those abuses are things of the past. At the same time I did hear the other day of a young lady who offered a cup of tea to an American gentleman, and be asked her the price of it. She said "It is Si now," and then she kissed it, and said "The price now is a guinea." He said " Waal I will give you the guinea, but I like my china clean, and I thank you to give me a clean cup." (Laughter.) That was a very un- gracious way of meeting the demand of the lady. Well, then,l think that very likely in former days there might be a species of what censerious people would call gambling in the way of raffles. Well, we shall dismiss that from the controversy because there is to be no raffling, i understand, in this bazaar, so that we at least 511311 not eacourage excessive betting on horse. racing or excessive commercial speculation, and we shall not bring the Church in the person of my friend Mr Yonge into cotillion with the State in the person of the Mayor in any controversy as to whether raffling, which I take it is the equivalent of the Old Testament custom of cast- ing lots,is as infringement of the Lottery Act. (Hear, hear.) Well, there may be something,and there certainly imomething said against bazaars; but the aegteraents in favour of bazaars are legion. I have seen institutions that but for the means raised by sales like this would never have attained to the success they did attain to; and when I remember what I have seen—institutions that owe their success as I say to sales of work like this, and the good that I have men done, the ignorance enlightened, the distress comforted, the religious knowledge imparted, I cannot but wish them suc- cess in the name of everything that is bane eolent and bone- icient. (Hear, hear.) It is sometimes said that young people who work for these bazaars do not work with that purity and singleness of purpose that they ought to do when they are working for religious and philanthropic pur- poses. Ido not believe this. (Hear, hear.). I have seen men and women working for bazaars with an earnestness and a zeal that could only be excited by appreciation of the important objects for which they were working, and by a desire to do the best they could to promote those objects. They had rather good authority for saying that whether we eat or drink or whatever we do we may do it in a devout and devoted spirit, and not long ago Mr. Spurgeon, who may be often quoted,! dare say, in this room, said he could eat and drink and smoke to the glory of God. (Hear, hear.) Well, I don't think he proposed. to be profane, and I don't think I am profane when I say it is quite possible to make pincushions and work slippers to the glory of Odd. It is sometimes also said that this is an expensive method of con- tributing, aad that religious people ought to contribute directly and without bazaars. Well, that is begging the question, because the question after all is if working far bazaars is not the very best way of giving. I remember some years ago opening a bazaar at Oldham, and among other things there MO a screen that had been made by half a dozen factory workers, boys and girls, all in their teens. This screen sold for £24, which was the price these young people pat upon it, but these young people could not have contributed to that bazaar the same amount of money in any other way. They could not have saved in three or four months or a each which was about what the screen realised for the de- sire and I am quite sure from the anxiety that they showed that they had been stimulated not by a desire to make a pretty screen, but by a desire to remove the debt which was hanging over their place of worship, and which was hinder- ing the usefulness of both minister and people. (Hear, hear.) Now I have undertaken that the opening of this bazaar shall not last half an hour, and I intend to conclude my speech, and! intend to a3k those who may speak here- after to help me to redeem the pledge that the ladies shall begin the sale of work at half-past two o'clock. I have no inure to say except this : I wish to bear my personal tea- timony to the kind courtesy of our Wesleyan friends dur- ing this bazaar. (Hear, hear.) They have made the bazaar easy for us in every way in which they could. Someone more closely connected with Wyclffe church will express the obligatton that the Wycliffs church and congregation consider they are under to our Wesleyan friends, bull could pot deny myself the pleasure of personally bearing my tes- timony to the kindly courtesy that they have shown to- wards us. (Hear, hear.) Well, now, as regards this bazaar my experience of bazaars is that they always realise more than is expected—(laughter)-3nd I hope it will be so en this occasion. Ycti see how largely the skill, and indus- try and kindness of the ladies have filled the stalls; Ills now for you to empty them. I think that before Thursday such a sum will be realised as will reward those who have spent so much labour upon it. I have made some inquiry and I find that the good policy has been followed of putting cheap prices on the articles so that I can tell every buyer that he or she will have money's worth for their money, and
NEWTOLCOMMISSIONERS V. THE

• WARRINGTON GUARDIANS. At the Warrington County Court, on •Tharsday, this Case came before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes.—Mr Walton, bar- rister, Liverpool, instructed by Mr Worsley, law clerk to the Newton Commissioners, appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr Wharton, barrister, Manchester, instructed by Messrs W U Jeans and Co., appeared for the defendants.—Mr \Yellen said the claim was one for expenses which had been paid by the Commissioners to the Guardians of Warrington in respect of hospital attendance and maintenance of Henry Harris, George Harris, Elizabeth Harris, and Afred Harris, from certain dates mentioned in the particulars. The amount in dispute was £3O 03 41 The Newton Corn mis- eioners were the Sanitary Authority for the district of Newton-in-Makerfield, which was a district within the Union of the defendants, the Warrington Board of Guar- dians. The corporation of Warrington had a hospital for infectious diseases, for the reception of patients suffering from such diseases, and the claim in this case was made in respect to expenses that had been incurred by the pl ai rat; ff s for the attendance and maintenance of the persons whom he had named, who were sent to the Warrington hospital from the Newton district. By section 131 of the Public Health Act. 1a75, it was shown that both authorities were local authorities.—Mr. Wharton did , not admit that his clients were a local authority within the Act, and Mr. Walton replied that authority meant urban sanitary authority, and his idea was suggested from the heading of their letters—" Warrington Union Rural Sanitary Authority." Couneel then read sections of the Act under which infectious diseases are dealt with. Under the Act, he said, the plaintiffs about the beginning of 1881 entered into an arrangement with the Corporation of Warrington for the reception by the Corporation of War- rington of cases from the plaintiffs district. The arrange- ment Was that they should pay a yearly subscription, and should also in respect of every patient sent make a pay- ment after a certain rate, so that when the Newton Commissioners sent anyone to the Warrington hospital, tney had to pay for each patient at the rate of 1.6 a per week, and the claim in this action was in respect of money so paid. No claim was made in resp.?ct to the annual subscriptiOa. His case Wlie that the patients in question were sent under an arrangement made between the plaintiffs and defendants, that arrangement being that In pauper cases the expenses incurred by the plaintiffs should be repaid to 'them by the deleadanh..—Mr Wherton, for the defence, con- tended that there had been Co Mich contract at Claimed by the other side, that the Guardians then, as now, resented to themselves the right to deal with pauper cases. The Newton Comthiseioners had nothing whatever to do with the jurisdiction of the Guardians. He also con'ended. that the cases in question were not pauper cases, and that had they been they should not have been removed without the attention of the Guardians haying been called to it previously. The Guardians had absolute discretion as to whom they would relieve, an no one could compel them by action at law to supply ABor C with relief. Any per- son who thought proper to supply a person with relief had no right to recover it from the Guardians.—Mr Caldwell, relieving officer, Newton, and Mr J C Sutton, c:erk to the Board of Guardians having been examined for the defence, his Honour adjourned the case, after a hearing of about six hours.

Of these applioants seven were chosen to compete, but only live presented themselves. Each can- didate, after performing on the organ a piece of his own selection, had to play and transpose at sight, improvise on a ziven theme, and harmonise a given melody. Mr. A. W. Sun- day Closing: Ine Clerk said a petition for Sunday closing had been sent to him asking that it might be signed by members of the Board, and then forwarded on to the Holmes of Farliament.—The Rev F Chambers said he was in favour of signing the petition, for they should try and preserve their Sundays from the way in which they were I disgraced at the present.—Father Finegan seconded. THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE ASHTON LOCAL BOARD.—The London and North- Western Railway Company were summoned by the Ashton Local Board, at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, for non-payment of a district rate amounting to £l9&.—Mr Clavdon represented the Local Board, anal Mr Croake, of Ruston, appeared for the company.—Charles Hodgkinson, rate collector, Ashton, produced the rate book made on the sth November, 1884. The amount of rate apportioned to the London and North-Western Railway Company had been demanded and not paid.—Mr Croake said that when the company received the demand note notice of appeal against the rate was given, and recognisances were entered into to take the matter to the quarter sessions at Liverpool. He therefore asked the Bence to dismiss the summons as the case was really before the court of appeal.—Mr dlaydon submitted that the Bench had no discretion, but to make an order for payment of the amount due. The rate had not yet been appealed against, but notice had been given, and if the company succeeded in the appeal they would get back any overplus they might have paid. The Board had already I offered four times to take the rate on the old assessment,' but the company bad made no reply,—The n?agistrates made an order for the amount claimed. DEATIL OF A LOCAL TRAINPMAN. —The somewhat sudden death of Mr Benjamin Franklin Kelly, tobacconist, of Queen-street, on Wednesday evening, caused the deepest sorrow among his many friends. Mr Kelly was only 23 years of age. In August last the deceasees mother died after a long illness, throughout which her son " Bea " attended to her with great devotion. The close attention he then bestowed upon his suffering parent, to the neglect of his own wants, brought on a severe cold, which rapidly induced an attack of consumption. For the last three months he has been attended by Dr Meunc'ey, of Earles- town, and Dr Fox of Warrington, but medical skill was unavailing. He became unconscious on Monday evening and never recovered. His remains will be interred at War. grave Church on Monday afternoon. The deceased was unmarried.
