TEST BY EVERTON.—Three weeks - ago in the final tie of the competition for the Liverpool and District Football As. sociation Challenge Cup, the Earlestown team defeated the then holders, Everton. by one goal to none, but the logers protested against the decision of the referee (Mr Hull, chairman_of the association), who disallowed an alleged goal obtained by Everton. The matter-was brought before the Committee of the association, who upheld the decision of the referee. The Everton Club, however, -have sines sent another protest to the committee, and asked them to- reconsider their decision. They urged that no direct evi- dence had been given ta them in reference to the alleged .goal. The second protest recently came before a well-atten- ded meeting of the committee, when it was unanimously decided that the protest by Everton be not reconsidered, and that the cup and gold medals be handed over to the Earles- town Club in laccordance with the result of the match,

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR NEWTON.
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR NEWTON.

The first meeting of the Executive Council of the Liberal " SOO " for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire was held in one of the rooms of the Earlestown and Dia- trict Liberal Club, Fairclough-street, Earleatown, on Tues- day evening, when there was a full attendance of represen- tatives, including Mr C Pilkington, J.P., Haydock, who presided; Messrs A C McCorqaddale. J.P. (Newton), Raw- lins (Rainbill), Neill (Bold), S Woods (Ashton), Beilby (flaydock), W Mitchell (Golborne), Roberts (Ashton), ?cc, Mr ctl croxden Of LiVerl)ool, elaa also present. The first busines6 *as the Ostilideratl9ll Of roles ter the guidallet of the " 300 " and the Executive NOM, and after some conalderation a code of rules drawn up by Mr Rawlins, of Rainhill, was unanimously adopted. Mr Powell next gave an Interesting statement with regard to the poll- ing booths that would be required in the division in the event of a contested Parliamentary election. It was stated that the Conservatives only wished for one polling booth for Haydock and Ashton, but Mr Powell explained that Ashton, from its size and population, would require to have at least two, and Haydock.would require one. He proposed to have one booth at Newton, and one at Earlestown, and the remainder of the booths in the other districts proportionate to the pop- ulation. The members of the Executive expressed them- selves in favour of Mr. Powell's suggestions, and adopted them. After a brief discuaaion on the work of registration, the question of selecting a Liberal candidate for the divi- sion was considered. The meeting appeared to be unani- mous that Colonel George McCorquodale was the Etost likely candidate that could be brought forward in the Liberal interest, and a deputation, consisting of the vice- presidents of the Association, was appointed to wait upon him to ask his consent to allow himself to be nominated. The Secretary was ordered to write to Mr. Itlceorquodale as to the most anavenient time for thail gentleman to receive the deputation. This. concluded the business.

div.head: ANTI-VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ANTI-VACCINATION AT EARLES- TOWN.
DISTRAINT AND SALE BY AUC HON.

The friends and supporters of the Earlestown branch of the National Anti-acenpulsory Vaccination Society had quite a gala-day on Monday. Though the locsl branch of the Anti-compulsory VacoNation Society' has b9en in exi3t- ence but a short time, and might almost be termed in its infancy, its members have gradually increawed, and daring the last few weeks friends ruxl supporters have rallied round it. Whatever opinions may be entertained as to the wis- dom of compulsory vaccination, on all ban& it has been admitted that the local anti-vaccinators had a remarkable success on Monday; and the anti- vaccinators have displayed enthusiasm over the result of what one described as-their first "pitched battle" with the local authorities. Ie June last a number of persons appeared at the Newton Town Hall to answer summonses charging them with fail- lag to have their children vaccinated, and in each case a penalty of 20s and costs—the highest possible penalty—was imposed. Free of the then defendants,.viz ,Messrs A Forster, Regent-street; R Higgins Market-street ; J Clarke, Bridge- street; W Gilmour Earle-street; and It Harrison, Earle- street, have since declined to pay the fine and costs, and also declined to have their children vaccinated. The result has been that the Board of Guardians of the Warrington 'Union, by whom the proceedings were first taken, instituted proceedings for the recovery of the amounts due. This was by levying distrainte upon the furniture and household goods of the parties named. The preliminaries were carried 1 outs fortnight ago, when police officers visited the dwell- ing-house of each person, and placed upon certain goodsel which it was expected would realise by sale by auction the amount due, a chalk mark, thereby impounding the goods. This created no little excitement among the local anti-vaccinators, who gave expression to their feelings in strong terms. Placards were posted and handbills were cir- culated throughout the town and district bearing the heading "-Stripping the homes of working-men, or legalised rob- bery !" Continuing, the bills stated " The goods of Messrs A. Forster, R Higgins, J Clarke, W Gilmour, and B Harrison,. who have refused to submit their children to the poisonous lancet of the vaccinator, through conscientious objections, I will be sold by public auction (due notice of the time and place of which will be given by the beliman on the day of sale, as the authorities are determined to keep us in the dark on that matter) early in the week commencing March 22nd, 1885, to pay the fines and costs imposed upon them by the Newton-le-Willows Bench, being the price demanded by an tan-English law for the privilege of keeping their children's blood pure and unadulterated. Collections," it was added, " will be made at the site and meeting to assist the friends in battling against this tyranny. We think this the beet way of advertising our good and noble cause, and we hope lovers of medical freedom will assist at this and future pro- secutions.' _ _ _ _____ _

THE " SALE : " AMUSING SCENES. Early on Monday the bellman rather surprised the anti. vaccinatore by an annaluncement that the sale of their goods would take place at three o'clock that afternoon in the yard of the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton. The holding of the sale at Newton and the consequent removal of the articles of furniture created some illfeeling. The whole police force of the district was told off to work as furniture removers. Police-sergeant Commins with five conetables under him I obtained a horse and lurry, and first visited the house of Mr Gilmour, at the far end of Earle-street, and consequently the furthest away from Newton, where the sale had to take place. The police then seized the 0 chalked" articles and placed them on the lurry, and ha subsequently transpired, took other articles which had not been previously marked, thereby, it is stated, exceeding their duty. This was dens at the residences of Mr Harrison, Earle-street; Mr A Fors- ter, Regent-street; Mr Higgins' Market-street ; and Mr Clarke, Bridge-street. As the police proceeded through the streets of the town with the impounded goods, they formed an object of amusement to large numbers of persons who gathered to witness the unusual occurrence. There was, however, no attempt at interference with them, About noon several prominent agitators of the anti-vaccination move- ment arrived from Blackburn and Wigan,. including Mr Thomas Danbury, of Blackburn. who has several times repre- sented the Earlestown anti-vaccinators in the Newton courts; Mr R Kilshaw, a prominent town's missionary of the temper- ance cause at Blackburn; Mr Alfred Gibson, auctioneer, Wigan, who took a prominent part at the " sale," and other gerttlemen. In be afternoon Mr Kilehaw, after sounding a monster wood rattle, proclaimed the "sale " in the streets of Earlestown and Newton. There was no doubt they would have paid their fines if they had been but is or 5e and costs, but their opponents idea of carrying out was 20s and coats, the very highest penalty they could impose. In June last Mr Sutton, the clerk to the Guardians, stated at the Newton Court that be would have to go on until all the sal-vaccinators In Earlestown were expunged, because there were only a handful ; but at his last appearance at the court he changed his story and told the magistrates there were 400' defaulters in Earlestown—(applause)—and he added that instead of having two or three cases there that morning there ought to have been 200. The gentle- man who was thus going to expunge them or snuff tlrm out found it was difficult than he expected. The more he tried to put them down the more the people would stand to their guns. They were now in the army and inten- ded to go on in- tho fight. They asked their friends to join their society and render all the assistance they could, for though they might not have children of their own lobe vaccinated, they would to helping to fight the battles of others. Ile advocated the claims of the anti- vaceination society, and concluded by asking them to tome forward and, show themselves on their side. (Ap- plause). Mr W Gilmour next gave an address. He said there was a common saying that auctioneers would do anything, but after that afternoon be did not think the auctioneers in Earlestown would do, anything. (Applause.) They had allowed their goods to be taken that day because they held conscientious objections to vaccination. He himself had suffered greatly from vaccination for a great many years, and would he not be stupid and foolish if he allowed them to vaccinate hie children, when he believed it would bring mischief and doctors' bills into his house ? Did they not think he was acting the wiser Dart in wanting to pay fines rather than doctors' bills? (Applause.) They were not alone or isolated upon that question. He saw from that day's evening papers there were some 50,000 people attend- ing an anti-vaccination meeting at Leicester, and did they think that number of people could be got together in one town unless there were some principle at stake 7 Alludieg to-the prosecutions he urged that the magistrates at Newton should exercise their discretion as in other cases, but the anti-vaccinators were merely asked if they were guilty or not guilty, and whatever they said they were fined 203 and costs. (" Shame.") It was a question affecting everyone present, and as many of them would have votes before long he would advise-them to exercise their votes in a proper manner and according to their conscience. He thought he bade perfect right to advocate that course of action. The Act for repeated penalties was only passed in the House of Lords by a majority of one vote, and that of a b;shop who casually dropped in and recorded his vote in favour of re- peated penalties. Repeated penalties was one of the things that wanted abolishing. (Applause.) They did not want to compel anybody else to have their children unvaccinated, but if they wished to vaccinate they could vaccinate their children every month or even every day if they liked. (Hear, hear.) The anti-vaccinators were fighting for liberty, and it was strange that that should be necessary in England in the 10th century. (Applause.) At this point a telegram was received, and on being handed on the platform Mr T Duxbury stepped forward and said: About seven o'clock we sent the following telegram to our friends at Leicester, where there are two or three Bodes. town friends to-night:—" Lancashire to the front. Five distraints at Earlestown to-day; eight at Nelson next, week. Capital meetings this afternoon and night; much sympathy. inquiry, and enthusiasm," And in reply we have received the following telegram from Mr Ellingworth, the anti. vaccination agent at Leicester :—"Greatest possible excite- ment here. Immense crowds. We Leicester people convey our hearty sympathy, and hope to-day's work brings a rich harvest full to overflowing." (Loud applause.), Mr W Gilmour (resuming) said if it could be proved that the friends of anti-compulsory vaccination could prove that they were injuring their neighbours' chilaven in any shape or form they would at once fall in with, their opponents' ideas, but until that could be done they were acting in the right in protecting their own children. (Applause.) Mr R Kilshaw, of Blackburn, who was next called upon, received a warm welcome. He remarked that he was, glad to see so many ladies present, because the hand that locked the cradle rocked the world. If the women of England would only do their duty on that question their yaks wauld ring throughout the length and breadth of the land, and make it impossible for medical despotism or interested ofd- dale to oppress the people by violating the sanctity of the English borne. SHE WAS AN ARTLESS THING.—" There is a ring in thoeel tones," said the girl who had been listening to the sweet whispers of her lover. AUNT JADE LETS OUT THE SECRET.—"AIIdt Jade, is it I quite true that a lady may ask a gentleman to marry her, if it is leap-year?' "Yea, ray dear, it is quite true." "Bet,' if he doesn't want to marry her, aunt Jane, what rend he de ' then ?" "He must give her a new black silk dress, my dear, and then she understands." "Oh, aunt Jane, aunt Jane, now I know why you have so many black silk dresses !" Scene--Bootmaker's shop with legend "Boots mended while you wait." Credulous party, handing in his boots: "Look sharp, now, and I'll wait." Bootmaker : " We're so full up of work, you can't have them under a couple of days." Credulous party: "A couple of days! Why you old humbug, you have it stuck up in your wiadow that you mend 'ern white people wait !" Bootmaker t "Just so; and, If you'll wait a couple of days, you'll have 'sea." GEORDIE ANSWERS A SYHPATHISER.-0110 stormy morn- ing, while a party of Scots were crossing from Arran to Ardrossan, one of the number was observed by his com- panions to be sitting at the side of the boat with a vary woe- begone expression on his face, and evideatly suffering severely from sickness. On seeing this, one of the travellers approached him, and said kindly, "Are you sick, Geordie ?" "Ma gudness," said Geordie, looking up in evident disgust, " d'ye think 'am doing it for fun ?" An anecdote is told of a man who in his time was a Cabinet Minister. There was a great discussion on the -question whether a man can marry on three hundred pounds a year. "All I can say," said the great man, "is that, when I said, 'With all my worldly goods I thee endow,' so far from having three hundred pounds, I question whether, when all my debts were paid, I had three hundred pence.' " Yes, my levee" said his wife; "bat then you had your splendid intellect!" "I didn't endow you with that, madam," sharply retorted the right honourable husband. I Mr. Edmund Yates, in his amusing Recollections and Experiences, relates that, after the succeesful prodaotlon of one of Jerrold's comedies, he, with other friends, warted him to the Bedford Hotel, where supper was prepared. "Jerrold," says Mr. Yates, "was flushed with triampb ; bat his bodily strength was small, and he hung ost to my arm. As we went up New-street, we met two or three drunken roysterers, one of whom, after tumbling up against me, apologised and asked the way to the 'Judge and Jury,' a popular entertainment of the day. Instantly Jerrold bent forward and addressed him: 'Straight on, young man; continue in the path you are now pursuing, and yon can't fall to come to them!'" As Ile WAS SATING.—At one of the theatres the other evening a man who had a seat between his wife and daugh- ter left it at the close of an act for a trip downstairs. When he returned he found a vacant seat two rows back between two women, and dropped into it with the remark : " As I was saying when I went out, it's none of your pudding what other women wear. Because someone else makes a fool of herself by wearing cotton stockings in the winter, it doesn't follow that you mast do the same." " Sir!" came from both sides of him at once, and the way he vacated that seat made the soles of his boots red hot. Nornrwo EXTRAORDIRARY.—The gallant Highlanders were stationed at Gibraltar. One night, Sandy McNab was sergeant of the guard, and in due course of duty had sent his corporal to make the last relief about four o'clock in the morning. While proceeding to one of the outlying posts the corporal missed his footing, fell over the cliff, and Was killed. Meantime Sergeant McNab had been filling up the usual guard report, preparatory to dismounting. Now, at the Not of the form on which such reports are Made oat there is a printed inquiry—" Anything extraordinary occur- red since remounting guard?" McNab, unaware of the accident to his corporal, filled this query up with the word "Nil," and, having no spare copy of the form, sent this one in to the orderly-room to take its chance. When the colonel and adjutant attended the orderly-room at ten o'clock, learned the mishap, and read McNab's report, the latter was peremptorily ordered to appear before them. "McNab," cried the colonel, in a rage, " what the devil do you mean by filling up your guard report in this way? You say Nothing extraordinary occurred since mounting guard, and yet your poor comrade fell over the cliff and was killed." Old Sandy, finding himself in a fix, pulled himself together, and after a moment or two of deliberation answered coolly," Well, sir, I don't see anything very extraordinary in that. It would have been something extraordinary, ye ken, if he hadna been killed." fie fell 800 feet. id di

MR. NORMAN, SEN., AND ECONOMY AT RUNCORN. Sir,—A " Ratepsyer " protests "that be never takes a mean advantage of an opponent ; " but in view of his cor- respondence, " methinks" this statement would be as diffi- cult to prove, as many others of which he is the author. Simply bccause the trustees of the Wesleyan Schools charge a re rtal for their buildings, my "honourable " oppo- nent " infers " that they " are ardent educationalists only so long as something can be wrung out of poor people." This inference is drawn with the full knowledge that when education was not so popular as it is to-day, these gentle- men gave without stint their time and money to secure its advantages to the poor; and I therefore repeat with empha- sis the ter.n unscrupulous. Stronger proof of the baseness of the charges against Mr Norman could not be adduced, than the well-known fact that in those dark days, when both subscription and collection were necessary, he was an earnest supporter of the schools, and strenuously opposed all idea of their transfer; and here I would again point out that his policy will only be press2d if no other means are adopted for controlling the conduct of certain notorious officials, whom I am decidedly of opinion may readily be curbed by well timed application to the Educational Board and the magistrate.' bench. Those of your readers who have followed this correapend- ence will doubtless have noted that every leading statement which "A Ratepayer" has made proves on investigation to be worthless. Dislodged from one false position, he has taken refuge in another, until driven to bay on every point he hurls broadcAst insinuations which no one can lay bold of. Despite his protests to the contrary, surely he is the vary Personification of meanness; and if in the future he again ply your readers with stricture' on public men, let me suggest that he ha brought face to face with the gentle- men he maligns, when I shall not fear for the latter's repu- tation. I note that my style does not meet with "A Rate- payer's" approval ; and while I retire to master and amend my faults of diction, let me commend to his consideration the important principles of honour and of truth.—Yours faithfully, VERACITY. March 24th. 1885. [With the ab*ve letter, we close the correspondence on this subject.—ED. Ex.]

THE FIRST PLEDGED TO rAL ABSTAINER : AN APPEAL. Sir,—On 291 h January last, " Old John King" died at Haw Lane, neu. S.mthport, at (ho ripe age of 90 years. He was tha first man in Great Britain who signed the pledge of total abstinence, on August 23rd, 1332. He WAS one of the pioneers of perhaps the most wonderful social movement of this century. , He took the step at a time when it was regarded as an act of madness; he dared to be "in the right with two or three," but he lived to see millions follow his brave example. Ile was staunch to his principles to the last. He and Joseph Livesey have conclusively proved that total abstinence and long life go together. Ttirough- out life he was a comparatively poor man, and for many years was station master at small stations on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Company's line. Owing to the failure of his eyesight. he was transferred in 1871 to Bescar Lane, where he had charge of a level crossing at the modest wages of 14s per we.ir, less Is 0.1 for rent. The work has, prac- tic thy speaking, been done by his wife, of whose unfailing devotion to her husband it is impossible to speak too highly. In 1373 it fell to my lot to make an appeal on be-. half of the old man, whom I have known for 23 year% and the result was that a sum of £230 was raised, which enabled ns to buy an annuity of £4O per year for the veteran. lie enjoyed this to the day of his death, and the Temperance Provident Institution has paid altogether £478 under the policy, generously paying up to the day of death, although not bound to do so by the policy. A few days ago I paid a visit to his widow, in the humble two-roomed house where they have lived for 14 years. She is still keeping the "pair of gates." but her wages have, in-consequence of her husband's death, been reduced to 53 per week, out of which Is 6cl goes in rent! Evidently this is not sufficient to keep body and soul together, and I feel stro iglv that some- thing should be at once done for her. She told me she was willing and anxious to work on as far as her strength per. ; but her work is very exposed, and her hours are very long. The gates require tending from 6-30 a.m. to 10 p.m ,and she is also liable t be called up at any hour dur- ing the night. And all this for 3s 6d per week ! The exposure to tbe we ither has already told upon her, and brought on serious bronchitis. I have been requested. through a letter in the newspapers, to make an appeal on her behalf; to such a reqlest I cannot turn a deaf ear. I feel certain that the temperance men and women in Great Britain, many of whom are numbered amongst your readers, will not allow John King's widow to remain totally unpro- vided for. I appeal to them very strongly, and ask that they will send me such subscription as they are able to affurd, for the widow of the faithful soldier who fought so long and good a fight. What is to be done should be done quiedy. I have had collecting cards prepared, and will glaily send them to any who are willing to help the fund by wait- ing upon their friends. All subscriptions will be duly ac- knowledged by me. If the mosey I receive will permit it, I propose to have an unpretentious stone placed over King's remains in Smthport cemetery. It is not fitting that such a man should depart and that no stone should mark his place of rest. It is eminently fitting that the 'temperance community should relive his widow and mark the place where lies a general who has for 33 years helped to lead a victorious army. I trust the response to my appeal will be I

such as to reflect credit en that large section of the commu- nity for whom King's pr nciples have done PO much.—l am, sir, yours truly, S. NORBURY WILLIAM. Chorlton-cum-Hardy, near Manchester, March 24th, 1885.

TRADE DEPRESSION: A FEW REMEDIES, Sir,—You were kind enough a few weeks ago to allow me to say a few words under the above heading; I wish to further supplement them. To a trading people, trade questions must always be of paramount importance; yet it must not be lost sight of that the agricultural interest may fairly lay claim to equal con- sideration with the trading interests when we are considering the nation's future welfare. England, as a consequence of 1 her geographical position, has in modern times led the way In all that makes up the sum of civilised life; her minerals and her hardy inventive sons have together been sufficient tog -e bet that prestige of which to-day we are so proud arm so tenacious. It must be a great satisfaction to the L 'wel and patriotic portion of the commueity to notice that the farming interest is at last being roue id up to a sense of duty. Since the Irish Land League was formed it has become the fashion for certain journals to decry all and every step that could be taken to force English landlords to listen to reason. "Liberty of contract " has become the watch-word, and the farmer has been strongly advised to have nothing to do with these revolutionary leagues, but to keep friendly with his land'ord and he will always be justly I dealt with. What has been the consequence? At eactly rent audit the farmer, with a supplicating whine, has beettl, compelled to plead poverty in the hope, the vain hope in '1 many cases, of receiving a pittance of his rent back again, and this is called " Liberty of contract." Lord Salisbury, to put off still further the natural solution of the problem, proposes to establish a kind of pawnshop, to which the far. user may go and pledge his grawing crops, and by this means make the landlord's income safe a few years longer. Happily he has been defeated in this original project. The "three profits" theory of Lord Beaconsfield, like his "pi ace with honour," does not stand the test of time. The tillers of the land mast not be called upon to provide a livelihood for the drones that own it. Bat now with respect to trade generally ; what is the outlook before us? It is at once granted that we have been the teachers of the world. English money, and English pluck, have made the term "Greater Britain" a well under- stood and accepted phrara, and Eoglishinen abroad send us cheap corn, make and import English machinery in America, Russia, and other countries. Englishmen manage and direct large manufacturing concerns that successfully com- pete with us at home. This is but the natural result of our , anxiety to make the English tongue predominant in the , world, and we shall have to abide by the consequences. 11Ir Woodhall, speaking at Stoke-en-Trent, said "that there was a levelling process going en all over Europe. The long hours of Continental workmen were being reduced, and the wages were being raised. Their diet was steadily becoming more getyrous, whilst the cost of animal food had increased in the came degree as in England. The competition of the future would consequently be a matter of skill, and the race would be won by the country which devoted itself most intelligently to the cultivation of its people, and especially of its youth. In plain English, this means we most not again expect to have things as we have hitherto had them." In my former letter on this subject I drew attention to an article on our Indian trade, written by a gentleman well qualified to speak on the subject. I refer to Colonel Phelps, Commissary-General of the Bombay Army. The argument of the article has been confirmed in a remarkable manner in a speech delivered by Mr. J. Jardine, chairman of the Board of Directors of the Manche ter Royal Exchange. Speaking of our Indian trade, he says : What was really wanted was an extensten of our mat kets. He should ike to see the same energy thrown into the open- ing up of new markets as was applie 1 to the power of pto- ducing. It was from this source he was convinced that pros- perity must ultimately come. There was no doubt that we had been in tlaa habit of looking to India to be able to take off anything thst we might be able to produce. We load there 200,000,000 of eeople, and it had been thought that by the.de- velopment of railways in India and by the general improve- ment of the country our Indian subjects would be enabled to relieve us of our extra products. But what did we find? We found that cotton mills were being established in India. He had j Ist race ved a note from Mr Lord, the ex-President of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce. in which he was Informed that the increase of crtton mile Is India during the last ten years amounted to 55 per cent. et the present moment 71 mills were actually at work and 10 were bong set to work. That was a fact which they had to leek in the face, end he could not help thinkieg GM India was now sot only supplying hereelf with a coarse fabric of cloth. but ' meeting us in Chins, Japan. and the smith of Africa. and the , time might come, if not before long, when India would be ab'e ' to produce the whole of that quality of shirting which bed been the staple trade of Lancashire, and which was known as B}lb shirting. It was rot only to the increase In the numeer of mills and in the improvement of their working that they bad t r look, but it was lobe remembered that the people employed be the Indian mi ls worked 25 per cent, longer hours and re- ceived less wages than the cotton operatives in this country, Be did h pe that, if India was not prepared f, take the pro- ductions of the English manufacturers, they, as traders, would lo et elsewhere for openings for their trade. He was glad to see the. Cnambers of Commerce had been drawing attention to this matter, and were endeavoueing- t o direct the mine of toe protrUc to fresh ruar wets. Africa and filteith America were no doubt favourable fields for future trade. It was there, in fact, that they must look for that ultimate improvement which would keep up the wages o our wort pe pie, and give that margin of profit to the manufacturer that was necessary to e able him to carry on his bminess su easefully. If it were true that we bad In the wo-ld 1,, 00 millions of population who were nct prod cars of tlielr own elothing, surely there was still a wide field for home pro- ducers. He need not refer to many of our old markets which were now ptect'cady closed against us, such as France. America, and Russia. They had almost closed their doors against art, and tele tesult had been t 3 give to the tra le of those ceentries a temporary stimulant. Ten years ago the entire cotton onnrumed in this country, in America, and on the continent of Europe was equally divided. We had 50 per , Cant and Eu op. and America 50. At the present time we I only consumed 40 per cent, while America and the continent of Europe ustel 60 per cent. The result of this increase of the ems tmption of cotton and the growth of mills was that America had ove taken her own requirements, and the Sims might be said of F arcs and Germany. In An:wrier, the mills were either standing or working short time, and wages had been lowered. That had been the result of protecting their own industries. Here we wanted nothing of that kind. We wanted more open markets. When we read such plain matter of fact statements as these, it were more madness to close our eyes any longer to the great necessity that exists for, in the first place, en- tirely overhauling the conditions under which our trade with India is carried on • and, in the next, recognising fully the importance of the growth of foreign trade, and the measure of its capacity in competing with us in foreign markets. CLIFFORD DIX. March 23, 1885.

LONDON, 'rricr TODAY.

_ - On Tuesday night, after long fighting against the possi- bility of war in Russia, public confidence subsided, and there was a regular scarce. In the House of Commons at question time Mr. Gladstone had been badgered in the customary mauler by the Ashrnead-Bartlett contingent, and there had been brought about that condition of mind which Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, next to the desire to advertise himself, chiefly has at heart. In the relations of private life, if a man be continually questioned on a particular point of family or social interest, and either flatly declines to give information er politely endeavours to give some crumbs of knowledge whilst withholding the loaf, there is a , natural tendency to fear the worst. It is believed that he is hiding semething either discreditable to himself, or disastrous to the community, or both. This is the effect in I the House of Commons even when such inconsiderable per. ems as Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, Mr. Onelow, or Sir Henry Wolff appear as questioners. Mr. Gladstone cannot, with due regard to the publie interest, frankly reply. He is too ; courteous to return gruff answers, and his wordy replies ' which answer nothing are regarded, on the Conservative side at least, as evidence of shuffling. It is a pity the Premier does not imitate the example of Lori Palmerston and Earl Russell. The former, of whose praise we hear a good deal in these days from Conser.vatiye lips, would have transfixed Mr. Ashmead Bartlett with a haughty stare if he had asked him in similar circumstances ' any one of the hundred questions with whioh the member for Eye nightly pelts the Premier. There is a tradition that Eta Russell once need an unparliamentary expression in • his angry refusal to answer a question put in the House of Commons on a delicate matter of foreign policy. Mr. Glad- stone need not swear. But it he were to meet malicious curiosity with absolute dumbness he would be sanctioned by the example of two of Me predecessors, and would re- ceiva the support of the House and the country.

Oa Tuesday night he had been quest7on-ed, and he answered in the usual fashion. Curiosity remained unsatis- fi .d, and the minds of members were open to any impres- sion. This was speedily conveyed in dramatic fashion. Toe Treasury Bench was filled with Cabinet Ministers at qeestion time. For a few minutes after the House went "into Co:nmittee they sat there. Then came a messenger from behind the Speaker's chair with a note which was passed from hand to hand to the Premier. As soon as he read it he whispered something to Mr. Childers, who sat on his left, and walked out of the House. Mr. Childers pasrecr the whisper on and also left, till all the Cabinet Ministers I were seen to leave the House in solemn Indian file. Ttien it was known that a Cabinet Council was being held in the Premiel'a room. Ministins assembled shortly after five o'clock. At six they were still in consaltatien. At half- past six, Inzads were solemnly wagged in the lobby, and it was said, with that assurance which sometimes accompanies absence of knowledge, that a despatch had arrived from St. Petersburg, in which British terms were fluted. It was nearly seven before the Cabinet Council broke up, and by that time everyone was certain that declaration of war was a matter of a few hours. The conviction in the House of Commons on Tuesday night spread into the city on Wt.& nesday morning, and thence was communicated to all the markets of Europe. There was something like a panic on the Stock Exchange, and prices tumbled down.

After all there was nothing in it. The Cabinet Council, which so dramatically gathered before the very eyes of the House of Commons, had been summoned early in the morn- ing. There had been no communication from St. Peters• burg of any kind, and matters actually stood as they had done twenty-four hours earlier, when the drift of opinion was in favour of the mtiutenance of peace. It is true that preparations for war are being grimly carried on both in India and England. But, as we have often heard, the best

General Grant is somewhat improved in health. He took a drive in the Central Park on Wednesday. THR OATHS BILL —Mr Bradlaugh has written to Mr Gladstone, directing his attention to the urgent necessity for the immediate passing of Mr Hopwood's Oaths Bill, the second reading of which has been blocked by Mr Warton and Mr P A Muntz. The Prime Minister replied that he fears he cannot at present give any other answer than he recently communicated through Lord R Grosvenor. The answer given by Lord R Grosvenor was that the Government could make no promire until good progress had been made with the Redistribution Bill. FUNERAL OF THR LATE SIR THOS. BAZLEY.—The funeral of the late Sir Thomas /3 izley took place on Monday at St. John's, Peansgate, Manchester. Notwithstanding that it was the expressed wish of the deceased that his interment should be of a private nature, sufficient publicity was given to show that the late baronet was universally esteemed and respected in Lancashire.—ln his sermon in the Cathedral on Sunday evening, Canon Stowell said :ir Thomas Eazley was a true gentleman, remarkable for his courtesy and kindness towards all with whom he came in contact, and was widely respected and esteemed for his unpretending Christian character.

ScrOESSFC7L LITBEPOOL NEwsraPgns.—The aphorism, .‘ nothing succeeds like success," has, happily for the pro- prietors, been fully realised in the case of the Liverpool Daily Post, the Liverpool Weekly Post, and the Liver- pool Echo. Those who take an interest in such matters have the advantage of consulting in another column the certified figures of the actual publication of these enterpris- ing and spiritedly-conducted papers. It will there be seen stated on the indisputable authority 0 Messrs. Harmeod Banner and Son, the well-known accountants. that the aver- age weekly circulation of these papers has reached, in so far as Liverpool papers are concerned, the unprecedented number of 650 092 copies. MRS WELDON kND M. RETIREE. Mrs Weldon was charged at the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday, with haying libelled M. Reviere. The defendant pleaded not guilty, and justified the alleged libel on the ground that it was true. Mr. Montagu Williams having opened the case for the prosecution, evidence was called in support, and it was speedily closed. Mrs Weldon addressed the jury in her behalf and called M. Reviere as a witness respecting the business transactions between them. The trial was. ad- jourred.—On Thursday, M. Rivi6re Was in the witness box throughout the whole of the day undergoing the process of examination at the hands of Mrs. Weldon. The hearing was again adjourned.—On Friday the Common Serjeant warned Mrs Weldon that she could not legally prove the truth of her charges against M. Riviera by reading the cor- respondence which had passed between them. She, how- ever, went on to examine M. Riviera upon the correspon- dence to show that he endeavoured to cheat her. THE ROYAL VISIT TO lIIIKLAND.—A.I a meeting on Sun- day of the National League, at Killemaule, the principal speaker was Mr Patrick•O'Rele, of Cashel, who was re- cently, under peculiar circumstances, a candidate for the Parliamentary representation of Tipperary. Adverting to the proposed Royal visit, he asked how could the Irish peo- ple give a welcome to the Prince of Wales, who was the head of the Freemasons—a body which was the avowed enemy of Catholicity all over the world and of nationality , in Ireland. At a meeting of the Dublin Municipal Council, ' on Monday, the Lord Mayor, replying to a question, announc ,d that, hay ng regard to the resolution adopted at the last meeting of the Corporation, when it was decided that no address should be prevented to the Prince of Wales, he had determined not to attend the ceremony of hying the foundation stone of the new Science and Art Museum by his Royal Highness. On Wednesday the Limerick Board of Guardians, by a majority of six votes to four, rejected a ,resolution to present an address to the Prince and Princess of Wales.

The loss of camels in 4 recent skirmishes around Suaktm amounts to no learthan 1100. The Prince of WEeriand Prince Albert Victor arrived in London on Friday (aliening from Brussels. The tan for the Liverpool Spring Cup resulted as fol- lows :—Chiselhurst, 1; Brocken, 2; Kilcreene, 3. Eleven ran. • Mr. Goschen has received an invitation to become a candidate for the representation of Glasgow University in Parliament. '

Nearly £B,OOO damage was done on Friday morning by a fire at Messrs. H. Marriott and Co.'s weaving and dyeing mill, Stockport. VVrtecx OFF LIVERPOOL. On Friday morning the schooner Eliza, of Padstow, laden with china clay, and bound from Cornwall to Gersten, was wrecked off the Mer- sey. The crew, after being six hours in the rigging, were rescued by the Liverpool lifeboat. They were landed at Liverpool at 10 o'clock in the morning in an exhausted state, and but partially clad. FATAL Boirate ExrLastcX.—Cei Fri 'ay morning, about nine o'clock, a terrible boiler explosion occurred at the brick and tile works of Mr. Archer, Coalville, near Leicester, by which one man was killed and great destruction of property caused. The buildings were partially demolishcd, a chimney stack blown down, and boiler plates cast a considerable dis- tance, a signalman on the Midland Railway having a nar- row escape. Subsequently the dead body of a workman, named Lager, was found in the debris dreadfully mutilated. The cause of the explosion is unknown. UNIVERSITY SPORTS.—These sports commenced at Lille Bridge Grounds on Friday afternoon in beautifully fine weather, there being an average attendance present The first event was hammer-throwing, which Orford won for Cambridge with a throw of ninety-nine feet seven inches. The hunched yards Cambridge was carried off by Boov, atter I a splendid race, in ten and four-fifths secs., for first time for fifteen years. The high-jtirc ping resulted in a tie, Hornby for Oxford and Purves for Cambiidge, both failing to do more than five feet six and a half inches. Oxford carried their first event in the mile race, Holland winning in 4 mine. 37 3•5 secs.; Waters (Cam- bridge), second ; Smith (Oxford), third. Oxford made things level again in the weight putting, Ware putting 38 feet 11 inches, and O'Kelly, the first of the other University, coming second. Blair, of Oxford, won the quarter mile event, there being a dead heat for the second position. McNeill (Oxford) easily won the hurdle race in 17 mine. 2-5 secs. Oxford won the broad jump with 19 .feet 10 inches; making certain of the odd event. The flea! event (three miles) was carried off by Eliot, of Cambridge.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The Select Committee sat on Friday for the last time prior to the adjournment for the Easter holidays, and heard further evidence given by engineers called by the petitioners, to the effect that the scheme of the promoters would create a fixed channel, diminish the storage capacity of the estuary, and interfere with the tidal scour which kept open the channel through the bar. Sir Frederick Bramwell, who was one of the witnesses, stated, in reply to the Earl of Milltown, that the depth of the lock sill at Eastham might be reduced without involving any other alteration in the plans of the canal. At the close of the engineering evidence as to the effect of the proposed works on the bar and on I Garston, the committee adjourned until Tuesday, the 14th of April. The Chairman said that when they met again the committee would like to hear counsel for the Mersey Dock I Board and the London and North-Western,Railwa, Dom- pany on these two points. They would then hear Mr. Pernber in reply on the same points, and afterwards con- sider whether they should go on with the •Bill any further. Mr Pope pointed out that this would compel him to-divide his speech into two parts; but he bowed to the decision of the committte.

div.head: OPPOSITION IN NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE.
div.p: OPPOSITION IN NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE.

The North Staffordshire Chamber of Commerce has de- cided to oppose the Manchester Ship Canal Bill on the ground that it deals with the waterway of the river Mersey in a manner to obstruct tha free use of the ports of Runcorn, Weston Point, and Ellesmere Port. It is stated that the chamber advocate the construction of a ship canal from Liverpool to the Potteries, or the alteration of the present Trent and Mersey Canal, so as to allow sea-geing vessels of small tonnage to go from Liverpool to the Potteries. DYNAMITERS' TRIAL.—COAMITTAL OF THE

div.head: PRISONERS.
div.p: PRISONERS.

At Bow-street Police Court on Friday, before Sir James logharn, James Gilbert Cunningham and Harry Burton were again brought up, charged with being concerned in the recent explosion at the Tower of Londoa.—Thomas Henry Adamson, Newcastle-on-Tyne, was the first witness called, and said he was a passenger on the Donau from New York to Southampton in February last year. Burton was a passenger on board the same vessel in company with another man, apparently a friend —Mr and Mrs Herrod, of Farndon, near Newark, also identified Burton as a fellow passenger.—William Henry Winn, incumbent of Barons- court, county Tyrone, said he travelled from Dover to Charing Cross on the afternoon of the Scotland Yard explosion. Before the train left Dever Cunningham got into the same carriage in a hurried, excited way.— Cunningham : You are a liar, you:never saw ma in your life before—Witness, continuing, said that Cunning- ham had with him a small black pelisse.—Folice Sergeant Cole, who came into the court on crutches and was ac- commodated with a seat, then gave evidence respecting the explosion in Westminster Hall in January last. He de- scribed the parcel which caused the explosion. On the top was a piece of what appeared to be boat-webbing, apparent-' ly intended for a band to 'secure the parcel round a person's waist. At one end of the band was either a button or a hook. The parcel could have been concealed under the cloak or great coat.—ln cross-examination, the witness said he did not think the parcel could have been better conceal-

ed by a woman than a man. Colonel Majmdie, Government inspectß of explosives, gave evidence, after which Mr. Poland, om behalf of the Treasury, asked the magistrate to commit the prisoners on the charge of treason felony, the penalty for which is penal servitude for life.—Mr. Quit Ham, on behalf of the prison- ers, reserved their defence.—The prisoners were then com- mitted for trial at the next sessions at the Old Bailey, to be held on the 20th April.

div.head: ITALIAN RED SEA EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE ITALIAN RED SEA EXPEDITION.

NAPLES, FRIDAY.—Tke flotilla of six torpedo boats, to- gether with the ironclad Ancona and the ironclad transport Conti di Cavour, which left this port for Massowah on the 25th ult., have entered the Red Sea. The medical officer for the floating hospital to be eatablisbed at Massowah left here yesterday for the same destination. The ironclad transport Citta di Napoli will sail to-morrow with material for the installation of artificers at Bilul and Mas- sowah.

_ THE FRANCO-CHINESE WAR. Paws, FRIDAY.—The unofficial estimate of the results of the defeat of the French in their advance from Dong Dang on the 24th, are much more unfavourable than those offi- cially communicated to the Chamber yesterday. The Gaulois says that thirteen officers are among the killed, and that the position of the French force is very precarious. There are 40,000 Chinese troops on the Tonquin frontier. The necessity for the despatch of adequate reinforcements is strongly urged by to-day's newspapers, and the Figaro ad- vocates a match on Canton.

div.head: SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.
THE IMPENDING BATTLE.

&TARIM, FRIDAY —The enemy fired some shots last night into the z4reba on the Tamal road, but no one was injured. General Graham will advance upon Tamai as soon as the water transport arrangements are completed.

Suagru, FRIDAY NOON.—Skirmishers are still actively engaged clearing the position for the advance on Tamai. The temperature here is very favourable for sick and wounded, who are all doing well. Captain Datrymple is progressing as well as can be expected. The postal corps has arrived.

The Central News Chatham correspondent telegraphs that quarters are being prepared there for a large force of the army reserves. The garrison is very weak at present in consequence of the large number of troops sent to Egypt and the Soudan. The greatest activity prevails in the ord- nance department in preparing the armament for the ves- sels ordered to be brought forward for commission, and ex• tra hands have been taken on. At Aldershot orders have been received to hold in readi- ness 25 men of the transport corps to embark for SinkiM on Wednesday next, the 17th company, on board the Ghoorka.

THE AFGHAN QUESTION RUMOURED ULTIMATUM TO RUSSIA.

The Globe of Friday publishes the following :—The im- portant communication forwarded by Lord Granville to St. Petersburg, on the 18th inst., was, we understand, a pro• posal that both the Russian and the Afghan forces should withdraw from the debateable zone pending the retult of negotiations at London. We are informed that a efinite reply arrived on Wednesday evening, refusing these condi- tions as being humiliating to Russia. A proposal, par- taking the character of an ultimatum, was telegraphed to St Petersburg on Thursday, with the request that the answer should reach Downing-street net later than Monday. 50,000 ADDITIONAL MEN FOB INDIA. A Calcutta telegram, in the second edition of the Times, states that 50,000 mer., under Sir Donald Stewart, are to tike the field at once, and further says that the force will be divided into two army corps of 25,000 men each, commanded respectively by Generals Hardinge and Sir F Roberts. The I reserve division of 10.000 wrong will also be mobilised. It ii believed that 15,000 men will be drawn from England; but preparations should be made to send at least 50,000 The utter folly of stopping the construction of the Quetta Railway is now painfully appar- ent. But, luckily, a good road has been made through the Bolan Pass. Supplies are being hurried up in large quantities. The preparations in India for the forward movement of troops are being undertaken In every branch of the Indian military service. Camels, mules, and horses are being bought throughout India ; and stores are being collected to supply 80,000 men in the field for a considera- ble period. Messrs John Brown and Co., Sheffield, who have in hand large Government contracts for railway material for India and the Soudan, have received urgent ordera from the

Indian Government to hasten forward with the utmost de- spatch the Indian work which is required jor the comple- tion of the Indian frontier lines for military operations. Sr. PETERSBURG, FRIDAY.—The German St. Petersburg Gazefte to-day states that communication has been estab- lished betweed eekabad, Sarakhs, and Merv. DRIFTING- TOWARDS WAR. The Central News says although no further despatches have passed recently between the British and Russian Government% and the situation remains diplomatically un- changed, yet events are drifting steadily towards war. The Government have now received full confirmation of the Russian intrigees in Penjdeh. These intrigues were ex- pressly designed to induce the Saraks Turcornans to rise against the Afghan garrison, but the Russian Government, whilst agreeing to suspend their advance, expressly reser- ved their liberty of action in the event of a disturbance At Penjdeh, which disturbance it is now admitted was actually being fomented by their accredited agent, Colonel Alikin- koff. Moreover, the British Government feels that the overtures which Russia has made for alliances againet Eng- land, not only to Turkey, but to other powers, and the terms which have been offered in return for such alliances being by ne means in accord with the pacific professions so constantly put forward from St. Petersburg. In addition to all this the natives of India are closely watch- ing the. progress of events on the Afghan frontier, where the Russian movements have caused considerable excitement throughout our Indian empire. India is now loyal and eager to render help, a fact suffici- ently shown by the large number of native recruits now flocking to our standards. From careful calculations that have been made it is estimated that Russia could net mass 25,000 troops before Herat until the middle of May, by which time England could throw a complete corps of 15 000 men into the place for its defence, besides having 50,000 in Afghanistan and the northern passes to support them within a month afterwards. These forces could be still further aug- mented,- but it would be absolutely necessary to draw 30,000 troops from Great Britain. If hos'ilities should be Commenced, the most competent military authorities hold that not less than 85,000 troops should be employed in a Central Asian campaign against Russia. CALLING OUT OF THE RESERVES. The Press Association understands that the Government do not at present contemplate calling out the whole of the army and navy reserves, but only in the first instance about 20,000 men of the first-class army reserve, and probably 5,000 or 0,000 Of the militia reserve. The army reserve now num- bers in all 39,224 men, and the militia reserve 30,134, mak- ing a total of close upon 70,000 efficient soldiers who are available for service at any moment. An estimate of the time it would take for the preparation and despatch of a large force was the subject of consideration last night amongst officers, and the highest authoriti-s believe that within ten days of the order being given 30 transports, selected from our mercantile marine, can be fitted and stored for the embarkation of 20,000 troops, including a fair pro- portion of cavil. y. It is the current ()Minion that 20,000 men will be at once put on a war footing, ready to start at any moment. Fifteen days will be required for fitting out this body of troops. The news of the calling out of the reserves has been re- ceived in Bolton with mingled feelings. There are about 1,000 first-class army reserve men in the town, who, whils.t welcoming the call to active duty abroad, consider that the pay to the wives and children left behind is inadequate, namely, fid for the wife and 2d for each-child per day. Large numbers of reserve and militiamen in Devon and Cornwall will be affected by the recent order, and their ser- vices are highly valued by their employers. Among the regular troOps the anpouncement is rec:ived with enthn- Maslen), as an indication of their being shortly called to . . active service. ' The Sheerness correspondent of the Central News tele- graphs that the Dockyard Authorities have been ordered to complete. H.M.S. Pylades, fourteen guns, for sea with all possible despatch. The Pylades is a new corvette, strongly equipped, and fitted with all the latest improvemen,s in shipbuilding science. The Queen's proclamation calling out the reserves is gazetted„

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. The Earl of Shrewsbury took his seat in succession. ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.—The Marquis of SALTS/1011Y wished to know whether it was understood that the Russian troops should remain he the present position until the demarcation of Afghanistan.—Earl GRANVILLE replied that the Russian Ambassador informed him that the lest despatch from the British Government was under considera- tion at St. Petersburg. There was every desire to come to a settlement satisfactory to Russia, India, and ourselves. Orders had been given to the Afghan troops not to ad- vance. THE EGYPTIAN LOAN—The Marquis of SALISBURY asked whether the foreign Powers had explained the reasons in- ducing them to require that guarantees to the proposed Egyptian loan should be international rather than p erely , British. Earl GRANVILLE explained that diplomatic I reasons made it desirable for the Government to depart from the original intention.—The Marquis of SALISBURY sug- gested that the foreign Powers would make their position, as guarantors, a weapon to interfere in the international affairs of Egypt. The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 4 o'clock. PHE ARREST OF ZEBEHR PACHA.—Lord E FITZHAURICE, replying to Sir H Holland, eaid Zebehr Pacha had been placed on board H.M.S. Irie and conveyed to Gibraltar, where he will be detained so long as the military necessity that caused his arrest continued. It was not intended to put him on trial. The noble lord, replying. to Mr Mitchell Henry, regretted that he could not answer his question re- parding the Afghan frontier. QUESTIONS —Lord R GROSVENOR, replying to Sir E Wil- mot, hoped to be able to nominate the Select Committee on Irish Industries before Easter.—Mr BRAND, replyine to Lord Elcho, said a searching inquiry would be made into the report of General Roberts' of the jamming of Martini- Henry rifle cartridges. That day orders had been given for the manufacture of solid case cartridges. THE SOUDAN CAMPAION.—Lord Mummer" replying to Mr Gourley, said it would be highly improper to cast censure on the officers on imperfect information, but re- port had been called on the attack made on the transport department of the army at Suakim on Sunday.—Sir D. WOLFF asked whether the Government, in view of the ter- rible massacre now going on in the Soudan, would consider expediency of informing the Mandi and Osman Digna what terms of peace they would be prepared to accept.—Mr. Gtemerroenz said he had already announced that any com- munications from the Mandi as to the terms of peace would be immediately considered, and he had nothing further to add to what he had already stated. THE CALLING OUT OF THE RESERVES —Lord HARTING- TON intimated that the messa:n calling out reserves would not be considered on Monday. The question of what classes of army reserves and militia should be called out was under consideration. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE. The adjourned debate on the Egyptian loan was resumed. —Sir M BEACH, in supporting Mr Bruce's amendment to Mr Gladstone's motion, insisted that the proposed agree- ment would inevitably result in incalculable mischief, both to Egypt and Egyptian interests, and instead of leading to a permanent settlement it merely postponed the day of reckoning for two years. He called on Parliament to reject the agreement, and thereby recover its freedom of action, which the Government had bartered away for a mess of pottage.—Mr CHAMBERLAIN defended the agreement, and urged the House not to follow the advice of the right hon. baronet, the result of which would be to defy and insult collective Europe. As to the argument that Liberals gave up their individual opinions in order to keep the present Government in office, It might equally be replied that the Conservatives con- cocted their convictions in orier to gain office. He con- tended that the Government were justified in entering into negotiations with the other Powe,s, and in making a bargain which, if it did not give us everything we could possibly have desired, gave us substantial advantages, and was the beat we could have expected. The Conservative party said they had an alternative policy, but as far as he could dis- cover the policy was an utter disregard of international and treaty obligations.—Baron DR Wolves condemned, and Mr SUTHERLAND approved the agreement. —Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON thought the value of the agreement was best shown by the lukewarm support that was given it by the supporters of the Government.—Mr. Seen°, while opposed to annexation, saw no reason why this country should not take a larger share in the affairs of Egypt, and he expressed the hope that we should either have the courage to stay in the country on terms honourable and sufficient to ensure good government, or else leave it to its own resources. [LEFT SITTING.]
The death is announced, at &liver, Suffolk, of John Prylie, an old Waterloo man. He had attained the age of 90 years.

, Mr H M Richardson has resolved to persevere in his can- didature as an " independent " Conservative for the borough of Bolton, the Council of the Conservative Asso- ciation having declined to accept hint as one of their candi- dates. SHOOTING k FATHER.—At Folkestone, on Saturday, a person named Inman went to a shop kept by his son to collect an account. A dispute arose, and young Inman fired at his father, wounding him in the arm. The would-be par- ricide then turned the revelver against himself and blew his brains out.

Kirkland Bros.of Bold-street, Liverpool, are the makers of these cakes, which were awarded the silver medal at the Health Exhibition. CREMATION.—Th& (sanatory which liss been erected at St. John's, Woking, was made use of on Thursday for the first time for the cremation of shaman body. The deceased was Mrs. Pickersuill, of Clarence-gate, London, and previ- ously to the cremation the remains were subjected to a post-mortem examination. • CONVICTION 05' A DYNAMITARD.—At Cork Assizes, on Monday, Judge Andrews sentenced Patrick Leary to twelve months' imprisonment for having attempted to blow up Mill-street Barracks with an infernal 'machine. His lordship said instead of twelve months he would give him twenty years, but that he was cortvinced be was only the tool cf the prinotpais ha the plot, w;bo, it was to he regretted, were *till at large '

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
SALE OF WOttli AT WIDNES.

A sale of work was opened in the Simrn's Cross School Chapel on Wednesday afternoon with the object of further reducing the debt upon the building. Toe chapel was erected at a cost of about £1,200. and the trustees are now struggling with a debt of £750. During the past few years nearly £4OO has been raised by sales of work, in the organi- elation of which the ladies of the congregation have always shown greet enthusiasm, and by the present effort it is hoped to obtain a further sum of £lOO. Although the chapel was founded by several earnest members of the Primitive Methodist Denomination only a few years ago, the accommodation is already insufficient to corn- fortably accommodate the children in atcendance 'at school, and the building is well filled every Sunday night by a devout coogregation. Under these circumstances it will be absolutely necessary to extend the building in a short time, and the hope of erect- ing a ckapel on ground adjoining, which has been secured with that view, will have to be indefinitely deferred. Cut- side aid would be highly appreciated by the zealous la- bourers at the chapel. There was a large attendance on Wednesday to witness ~the opening ceremony, amongst those present being the Rev J Calvert (stiprinten- dent minister), Warrington ; Messrs T J Peters, J H Lee, R Booth, 8 Owens, S Draught, Riuyard. Rollason, clic. Mr Joseph Hales, of Liverpool, had been announced to open the sale, but from some unexplained cause be failed to arrive, and the ceremony was performed in a very genial manner by Mr T J Peters, who was heartily thanked on the motion of Mr S Owens, seconded by Mr Drought. The sales were then commenced. The general stall, laden with a variety of articles of needlework, the work of the sewing meeting, was in charge ef Mrs Rollacan, Mns Lea, Mrs Bedgood, Mrs Williams, Mrs Drought, and Miss Wiles. A stall contaiu. lug fancy and useful articles of various descriptions, was attended to by MIS Adams, Mies Fanny Wiles, and Miss Balker. The refreshment stall was presided over by Mrs Wiles, Mrs Pinchers, Mrs Crossley, and Mrs Sage; and the tea table by Mrs Bradshaw, Mrs Room, Mrs Jones, Mrs Webster, and Mrs Hughes, The toy stall wag in charge of Miss Dinah &Mason and Miss Webster. The sale of work was continu^d on Thursday afternoon. In the evening a tea meeting was held under the presidency of Mr S Dutton, of Chester, and there was a good attend- ance. Mr Joseph Hales was present, and explained the reason of his absence on the previous day. He congratu- lated the congregation of Simm's Cross Chapel on the pro- gress they had made, and announced that the sale of work had realised £B3 He did not think they should be content with less than £lOO He had already- given £5, and he would give another £5 if the chairman would follow his example. ( Applause.)—The Chairman promised to do so, and the desired amount was raised. The following dona- ns were also given :—Mr Rollason £4, Mr S Owens £4, Mr B Brown £1 —Addresses were delivered by the Rev J Pickwell, of Runcorn, and the Rev E. Yeatman (Baptist). The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: BETHESDA CONJHEGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.
div.p: BETHESDA CONJHEGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.

On Sunday morning and evening the Rev. F. Barnes, of Cheater, preached in this chapel to good congregations, and collections were made in aid of the manse fund. After the evening service the sacred cantata" Daniel " was rendered by the choir, assisted by a number of musical friends. Mr W Handley conducted, and Mr Havenscroft presided at the organ. The principal eharacters were represented as fol- lows :—Queen, Miss Horton ; Sister of Aztriab, Mist N Handley •, Azariah, Mr R Norris • Daniel, Mr F Fair- hurst ; King, Mr Littler; Herald, Mr It Moore. The cantata was interpreted in a manner which gave apparent pleasure to the large congregations that had assembled.

On Wednesday—evenin-g the annual congregational tea party was held in the schoolroom, and there was a good at- tendance. The following ladies and gentlemen had charge ef the arrangements and attended to the tables :—Mesdames Wylie, liaziehurst, W Handley, Hetherington, G Lacy, Dobson, Ainsworth, and Williams ; Miss N Handley, Miss M IT Chadwick ; Messrs R Wylie, W 11 Chadwick, and Dobson. At the subsequent meeting there was a good audi- ence. The Rev J D lbornas presided, and there were epon the platform the Revs T Ballet Wlllir-ns (of Buckley), it Hughes (of Widnes), E WI hams (Presbyterian), and W Vann (Free Church). During the evening a choir, under the leadership of Mr W Handley, sang several glees in a pleasing manner.—The Chairman, in his opening address, expressed his pleasure that there were so many present t',lat evening, and that they were met under tolerably favoura- ble circumstances. They were at peace, and in the enjoy- ment of happiness and a great measure a religious privileges which they highly valued. During the past year they had - sustained very serious losses. Some of their best helpers in a monetary sense had died, others had left the neighbourhood for other localities, and within the last 18 months something like 40 adults had left the con- gregation for other parts. This was a serious matter for a congregation like theirs. He was, however, fully convinced that if each member took that interest which he or she ought to take that the gaps which had been made would be very soon filled up. He was thankful to know that dueng the present quarter of the year two or three families had
